13973.s: This order sets the line of succession for who may act as Environmental Protection Agency Administrator if both the Administrator and Deputy Administrator die, resign, or cannot do the job. It lists EPA officials in order and says they must be eligible under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act. It also revokes Executive Order 13763.

13974.s: This order changes an earlier order that restricts certain securities tied to Communist Chinese military companies. It allows some United States persons more time to sell those securities before ownership is prohibited. It also changes how Communist Chinese military companies are defined and says a “transaction” means the purchase or sale of a publicly traded security.

13975.s: This order encourages the U.S. Postal Service to consider changes to its buying rules so they match federal rules on price differences and when materials are treated as foreign. It says USPS should consider amendments to its Supply Principles and Practices after final rules are issued for the Federal Acquisition Regulation. The order applies to USPS procurement policies and does not change USPS authority or create a right anyone can enforce.

13976.s: This order creates the Wildland Fire Subcabinet to improve coordination on federal wildland fire management policy and oversight. It includes leaders from several federal agencies and is directed to meet quarterly. The subcabinet must identify and recommend ways to coordinate or consolidate related federal working groups, and it must develop a strategic plan with goals, performance measures, and reporting. It also addresses wildfire response, hazardous fuels, post-wildfire rehabilitation, workforce issues, and coordination with state, local, tribal, and other partners.

13977.s: This order directs the federal government to add protections for federal judges, prosecutors, and law enforcement officers, including their families. It tells agencies to remove obstacles for current and retired federal law enforcement officers to carry concealed firearms under the law, and it tells the Attorney General to propose rules for federal prosecutors to get special deputation to carry firearms when they face a risk of harm. It also calls for steps to reduce public access to home address and other personal information, and to propose legislation for more protection for these officials.

13978.s: This order revises earlier direction on the National Garden of American Heroes and tells the Secretary of the Interior to find a suitable site and move forward with construction there, as allowed by law. It calls for the garden to include statues of many named Americans. It also provides for funding, asks certain agencies to help commission statues, and requires an annual public report on progress until the garden is finished.

13979.s: This order directs federal agencies to require that rules under section 553 be signed by a senior appointee, and that only senior appointees may start the rulemaking process or approve the agency’s regulatory agenda. It also requires agencies to review their rulemaking delegations and update their procedures to fit these rules. Agencies must review significant rules issued over the last 12 years to see whether a senior appointee issued them and report the findings to the President.

13980.s: This order tells federal agencies to be clear when new rules can lead to criminal penalties and to state the mental state required, or say when a rule is a strict liability offense. It also tells agencies to give guidance on handling regulatory offenses through administrative or civil enforcement instead of criminal referrals when appropriate. The order focuses criminal enforcement on people who know what the rule requires or forbids and choose not to comply.

13981.s: This order directs federal agencies to review their authority to stop buying or funding certain unmanned aircraft systems made by or using parts or software from foreign adversaries. It also requires agencies to report on the UAS they own or operate that are made by foreign adversaries or have major parts from them. The order directs the FAA to propose rules on using UAS on or over critical infrastructure or other sensitive sites, and it tells agencies to treat replacing covered UAS as a budget priority.

13982.s: This order directs the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, with the Secretary of Defense, to consider whether veterans who served in Uzbekistan between October 1, 2001, and December 31, 2005, should be treated as veterans who served in a theater of combat operations. It also requires the Secretary of Defense to study possible toxic exposure at Karshi-Khanabad Air Base during that period and report the findings. The study must look at base conditions, health effects, and any link between toxic substances and those health effects.

13983.s: This order revokes Executive Order 13770, which was called "Ethics Commitments by Executive Branch Appointees." It says employees and former employees subject to those commitments will no longer be subject to them after noon on January 20, 2021.

13984.s: This order directs the Secretary of Commerce to propose regulations that would require United States IaaS providers to verify the identity of foreign persons who obtain accounts and keep records about those accounts. It also would let the government impose special measures on accounts linked to foreign jurisdictions or foreign persons found to be involved in malicious cyber-enabled activities. The order calls for recommendations to increase voluntary information sharing and collaboration among IaaS providers and with government agencies.

13985.s: This order directs federal agencies to work toward equity and equal opportunity for all, including people of color and other underserved communities. It requires agencies to review their programs and policies for barriers to access, report their findings, and make plans to address problems in benefits, services, contracting, and procurement. It also creates a working group on equitable data and revokes two earlier executive orders.

13986.s: This order directs that the census apportionment base include all persons living in each state, without regard to immigration status. It also requires the Secretary to use those totals in reports to the President and to state officials for apportionment and districting. The order says the population data must be accurate and revokes two earlier directives about citizenship status and illegal aliens.

13987.s: This order creates a COVID-19 Response Coordinator and a Deputy Coordinator in the White House. It directs the coordinator to help organize the federal response to COVID-19, including testing, vaccines, supplies, and support for schools and child care providers. It also orders steps on global health security, biodefense preparedness, and review of biological threats and pandemic readiness.

13988.s: This order directs federal agencies to review and, if needed, revise or replace agency actions that may conflict with the policy against discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. It says agencies should fully enforce laws that prohibit sex discrimination and consider steps to address overlapping discrimination based on race or disability. It applies to federal agencies and their programs, rules, guidance, and other actions.

13989.s: This order requires many executive branch appointees to sign an ethics pledge when they enter government service. The pledge bans gifts from registered lobbyists, limits work on matters tied to a former employer or client, and places limits on certain post-government lobbying and communications. It also says hiring decisions must be based on qualifications, competence, and experience. The order applies these rules through agency ethics procedures and allows written waivers in some cases.

13990.s: This order directs federal agencies to review recent regulations and other actions that may conflict with its policy goals and to consider suspending, revising, or rescinding them. It also calls for review of national monument boundaries, a temporary moratorium on federal activities tied to the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge oil and gas leasing program, and reinstating certain offshore withdrawals from oil and gas drilling. The order creates a working group to publish estimates for the social cost of carbon, nitrous oxide, and methane for use in federal decisions.

13991.s: This order directs federal agencies to require masks, physical distancing, and other CDC public health measures for on-duty or on-site federal employees, federal contractors, and people in federal buildings or on federal lands. It also tells agencies to provide guidance, allow exceptions when needed by law, and seek to provide masks when needed. The order creates a task force to guide federal workplaces on COVID-19 safety, testing, telework, and related matters.

13992.s: This executive order revokes several earlier executive orders about federal regulation. It tells federal agencies and the Office of Management and Budget to stop or roll back orders, rules, guidelines, and policies that carried out those revoked orders, if allowed by law. It also says certain positions, committees, task forces, and other entities created under those orders should be abolished where appropriate.

13993.s: This order resets how the government enforces civil immigration laws. It says enforcement should focus on national and border security, the humanitarian challenges at the southern border, public health and safety, and due process of law. It also revokes a 2017 immigration order and directs agencies to review actions taken under it and issue revised guidance if needed.

13994.s: This order directs executive departments and agencies to share COVID-19-related data, with protections for confidentiality, privacy, law enforcement, and national security. It also tells officials to review how public health data systems work, how data is collected and shared, and how to improve open data and hiring for data and information technology roles. The order covers federal agencies and also refers to State, local, Tribal, and territorial authorities.

13995.s: This order sets up a COVID-19 Health Equity Task Force in the Department of Health and Human Services. The task force is to make recommendations on how to use COVID-19 resources, relief funding, communication, and data collection in a way that addresses health inequities for communities of color and other underserved populations. It also directs federal agencies to review pandemic response plans, strengthen anti-discrimination enforcement, and work with state, local, Tribal, and territorial officials on food, housing, child care, income support, contact tracing, and vaccine outreach.

13996.s: This order sets up a federal board to coordinate COVID-19 testing and advise on expanding testing, lab capacity, and public health staffing. It focuses on testing for healthcare workers, schools, child care settings, long-term care facilities, correctional facilities, immigration custodial settings, detention facilities, food processing and manufacturing facilities, people experiencing homelessness, migrants, and seasonal workers. It also directs agencies to help make COVID-19 testing free for people without comprehensive health insurance and to expand access to testing and contact tracing.

13997.s: This order directs federal agencies to improve the nation’s ability to treat COVID-19 and to expand access to quality and affordable healthcare. It calls for plans to support studies of COVID-19 treatments, including research in rural hospitals and research on the long-term effects of COVID-19, and to consider including historically underrepresented groups in clinical trials. It also directs agencies to support care facilities, review needs at federal care facilities, expand access to programs for people recovering from COVID-19, and help improve the production, distribution, and insurance coverage of COVID-19 treatments.

13998.s: This order directs federal agencies to require masks on certain domestic travel, including airports, commercial aircraft, trains, ferries, intercity buses, and other public transportation, following CDC guidelines. It also tells agencies to look at additional public health measures for domestic travel and to support mask-wearing and physical distancing on public transportation. For travel into the United States, it sets a policy of requiring a recent negative COVID-19 test when feasible and following other CDC travel guidelines, including possible self-quarantine or self-isolation after entry.

13999.s: This order directs federal officials to take steps to protect workers from COVID-19. It calls for updated workplace safety guidance, possible emergency standards on masks and other COVID-19 protections, and a review of OSHA enforcement. It also directs outreach to workers and coordination with states, public employee unions, and other agencies to better protect public sector workers and other workers not covered by the Occupational Safety and Health Act.

14000.s: This order directs federal agencies to help schools, child care providers, Head Start programs, and colleges reopen and keep operating safely during the COVID-19 pandemic. It tells agencies to give guidance, technical help, data, testing materials, and other support for in-person learning, contact tracing, and child care. It also calls for attention to learning loss, mental health, family support, and unequal impacts on students and educators.

14001.s: This order directs federal agencies to review the supply of critical materials, treatments, and supplies needed to combat COVID-19, including protective equipment and supplies for tests and vaccines. It also calls for reports on shortages, stockpiles, pricing, and ways to improve distribution and production. The order affects federal agencies and also calls for coordination with state, local, Tribal, and territorial authorities, health care workers, health systems, patients, and Tribal health providers.

14002.s: This order directs executive departments and agencies to identify actions they can take under existing authority to address the economic crisis caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. It tells agencies to consider ways to improve access to programs, reduce unnecessary barriers, and better coordinate programs funded by the federal government. It also says agencies should prioritize relief for individuals, families, small businesses, and state, local, Tribal, and territorial governments.

14003.s: This order revokes Schedule F and several other executive actions on federal labor and removal rules. It tells agency heads to negotiate over certain collective bargaining subjects and to have subordinate officials do the same. It also directs the Office of Personnel Management to report on ways to promote a $15-an-hour minimum wage for federal employees.

14004.s: This order says all transgender individuals who want to serve in the U.S. military and can meet the standards should be able to serve openly and without discrimination. It revokes two earlier presidential memorandums about military service by transgender individuals. It also directs the Defense Secretary and Homeland Security Secretary to update their policies, stop involuntary separations or denials of reenlistment based on gender identity, review affected records, and let some people try to rejoin if they meet current entry standards.

14005.s: This order tells federal agencies to use federal spending and procurement to increase the use of goods, products, materials, and services made in the United States when allowed by law. It creates a Made in America Office in the Office of Management and Budget to review waiver requests and make some waiver information public. It also asks agencies to review actions that do not fit this policy, report on their use of Made in America laws, and consider changes to federal procurement rules. The order revokes some earlier executive orders and supersedes parts of others that conflict with it.

14006.s: This order directs the federal government to phase out its reliance on privately operated criminal detention facilities. It tells the Attorney General not to renew Department of Justice contracts with those facilities, as allowed by law. It applies to people in the federal criminal justice system and to correctional staff at those facilities.

14007.s: This order establishes the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, or PCAST. The council advises the President on science, technology, and innovation, and on scientific and technological information used for public policy in areas like the economy, education, energy, the environment, public health, national and homeland security, and racial equity. It may have up to 26 members, and it will end 2 years after the order unless the President extends it.

14008.s: This order makes climate change a central part of U.S. foreign policy and national security. It directs agencies to develop climate strategies, risk analyses, and a climate finance plan, and it calls for work with other countries on emissions, clean energy, and climate-related financing. It also creates a White House Office of Domestic Climate Policy to coordinate domestic climate policy across the federal government.

14009.s: This order says the administration's policy is to protect and strengthen Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act and make healthcare more accessible and affordable. It directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to consider a Special Enrollment Period for uninsured and under-insured Americans to seek coverage through the Federally Facilitated Marketplace. It also orders agencies to review existing actions that may affect Medicaid or the ACA, and it revokes two prior executive orders related to the ACA.

14010.s: This order directs agencies to make a regional plan to address the causes of migration in North and Central America and to improve asylum systems and other protection programs in the region. It also tells agencies to review ways to expand lawful migration paths to the United States for people from the Northern Triangle and to improve processing for refugees, visa access, and family reunification. The order also directs steps to restore and change border asylum processing, including reviewing Migrant Protection Protocols and revoking several prior immigration orders and memoranda.

14011.s: This order creates an interagency task force to help reunite children who were separated from their families at the United States-Mexico border. The task force must identify those children and make recommendations on reunification, including possible immigration benefits, services, and support. It must also give regular reports to the President and is directed to help prevent the government from repeating the policies and practices that led to family separation.

14012.s: This executive order tells federal agencies to review legal immigration rules and look for barriers that make it harder to get immigration benefits. It also directs them to review public charge policies and to make the naturalization process more accessible and efficient for eligible people. The order creates a task force on New Americans and revokes a 2019 memorandum on sponsors of aliens.

14013.s: This order directs agencies to rebuild and expand the refugee admissions program and improve how humanitarian programs are run. It also calls for better security vetting, fraud detection, transparency, and faster processing for refugee applicants, including people who are more vulnerable to persecution. The order revokes two earlier orders and a presidential memorandum, and it requires reviews of the Iraqi and Afghan special immigrant visa programs. It also directs agencies to consider ways to help refugees and other applicants get access to records, interviews, and other procedures.

14014.s: This order blocks property and property interests of certain foreign people tied to the Burmese economy, the military or security forces, or actions that undermine democracy, threaten stability, or involve human rights abuse in Burma. It also bans transactions that try to evade the order or give funds, goods, or services to or from blocked persons. The order suspends the entry into the United States of noncitizens who meet those criteria, unless an exception is made by the Secretary of State or the Secretary of Homeland Security.

14015.s: This order creates the White House Office of Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships within the Executive Office of the President. The office is meant to coordinate federal work with faith-based and secular community organizations to help serve people in need. It also changes several earlier executive orders and revokes a 2018 order that created the White House Faith and Opportunity Initiative.

14016.s: This order revokes Executive Order 13801, which had expanded apprenticeships in America. It directs the Office of Management and Budget and executive departments and agencies to consider rescinding related orders, rules, guidelines, and policies, and to abolish any related personnel positions, committees, task forces, or other entities.

14017.s: This order directs federal agencies to review risks to U.S. supply chains and to report on them. It calls for reports on semiconductors, batteries, critical minerals, pharmaceuticals, defense, public health, information and communications technology, energy, transportation, and agriculture. It also asks for recommendations on how to make supply chains more resilient and how to coordinate future government action.

14018.s: This order revokes several earlier presidential actions on financial regulation, poverty, labor-management authority, regulatory relief, funding to certain state and local governments, federal civic architecture, and agency rulemaking. It also directs agency leaders to consider rescinding any related orders, rules, regulations, guidelines, or policies, as allowed by law. Any personnel positions, committees, task forces, or other entities created under those actions are to be abolished, as appropriate and consistent with applicable law.

14019.s: This order directs federal agencies to expand access to voter registration and election information, and to work with state, local, Tribal, and territorial officials to remove barriers to voting. It tells agencies to review how they can help people register, request vote-by-mail ballots, and get multilingual election information, and it directs the General Services Administration to modernize Vote.gov. It also calls for steps to help voters with disabilities, active-duty military members and overseas citizens, eligible people in federal custody, and Native American voters.

14020.s: This order creates a White House Gender Policy Council within the Executive Office of the President. The Council is to coordinate federal efforts to advance gender equity and equality, including work on workplace fairness, education, health care, gender-based violence, and economic opportunity. It also directs agencies to review programs and policies for consistency with a government-wide strategy and to report on progress.

14021.s: This order says students should have an educational environment free from discrimination based on sex, including sexual harassment and sexual violence, sexual orientation, or gender identity. It directs the Secretary of Education to review agency actions and issue new guidance if needed. It also tells the Secretary to consider additional enforcement actions to enforce sex discrimination rules and to support students who have experienced discrimination.

14022.s: This order ends the national emergency declared in Executive Order 13928 about the International Criminal Court and revokes that order. It also ends the suspension of entry as immigrants and nonimmigrants for people covered by that order. The order says this does not affect pending cases, past acts, or penalties already incurred.

14023.s: This order creates a Presidential Commission on the Supreme Court of the United States. The Commission may have up to 36 members appointed by the President, and they must include constitutional scholars, retired federal judges, or others with experience and knowledge of the federal judiciary and the Supreme Court. It must gather public comment and other expert views, then send the President a report on Supreme Court role, history, and reform proposals.

14024.s: This order declares a national emergency over certain harmful foreign activities of the Government of the Russian Federation. It blocks property and property interests of certain people and entities linked to those activities, and it restricts transactions with them. It also suspends the entry of noncitizens who meet the order’s criteria, unless an official decides their entry is not contrary to U.S. interests.

14025.s: This executive order sets a policy to encourage worker organizing and collective bargaining. It creates a task force to identify federal policies, practices, and programs that could support worker power, including for workers in the private sector, State and local governments, and the Federal Government. The task force is also to look at workers who have not historically been able to unionize and at marginalized workers, including women and persons of color. It revokes two prior executive orders about the President's National Council for the American Worker.

14026.s: This order raises the hourly minimum wage for certain federal contractors and subcontractors. It applies to covered workers on federal service and construction contracts, some concessions contracts, and some contracts tied to federal property or lands, and it also sets rules for tipped workers. The order also directs agencies to add contract clauses, issue regulations, and enforce these wage requirements.

14027.s: This order creates a temporary office in the Department of State called the Climate Change Support Office. It is meant to help with U.S. diplomatic work on climate change and to support efforts in international meetings and foreign policy. The office may also work on topics like clean energy, aviation, shipping, the Arctic, the ocean, sustainable development, and migration.

14028.s: This order tells federal agencies to improve cybersecurity across their systems and to work more closely with private contractors and cloud service providers. It requires more sharing of cyber threat and incident information, including reports about cyber incidents involving software products or services used by agencies. It also directs agencies to move toward Zero Trust Architecture, use cloud services in a more secure way, and adopt multi-factor authentication and encryption for data at rest and in transit.

14029.s: This order revokes several earlier presidential orders on online censorship, monuments and statues, foreign assistance branding, the National Garden of American Heroes, and overcriminalization through regulatory reform. It also directs agencies to consider rescinding rules and policies tied to those orders and to abolish related positions, committees, task forces, or other entities where allowed by law. The order updates civil service rules to reflect the revocation of Schedule F and to list certain positions in Schedules A through E.

14030.s: This order directs federal officials to develop a government-wide strategy on climate-related financial risk. It asks agencies to measure, assess, mitigate, and disclose that risk for federal programs, financial markets, workers’ pensions, lending, underwriting, procurement, and the federal budget. It also reinstates the Federal Flood Risk Management Standard and directs some agencies to consider climate-related risk in their actions.

14031.s: This order creates a President’s Advisory Commission and a White House Initiative on Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians, and Pacific Islanders. They are meant to help the federal government advance equity, justice, and opportunity for these communities. The order calls for work on issues like hate incidents, language access, data collection, health, education, housing, jobs, and access to federal programs and services.

14032.s: This order blocks United States persons from buying or selling certain publicly traded securities tied to listed Chinese companies and to companies that operate in the defense, related materiel, or surveillance technology sectors of the People’s Republic of China. It also covers companies owned or controlled by those companies or by people listed in the order. The order expands the national emergency to include Chinese surveillance technology used outside the PRC or used to help repression or serious human rights abuse.

14033.s: This order blocks property and interests in property in the United States for certain people tied to actions that threaten peace, security, stability, or territorial integrity in the Western Balkans. It also covers people involved in undermining democratic processes or institutions, breaking certain regional agreements, serious human rights abuse, corruption, or helping blocked persons. The order suspends the entry of noncitizens who meet these criteria, unless the Secretary of State or the Secretary of Homeland Security decides their entry is not contrary to U.S. interests.

14034.s: This order revokes three earlier executive orders about TikTok, WeChat, and other software linked to Chinese companies. It directs federal agencies to remove or end actions tied to those orders and requires the Secretary of Commerce to study risks from connected software applications tied to foreign adversaries. It also calls for reports on protecting Americans' sensitive data, including personal health information, genetic information, and personally identifiable information.

14035.s: This order directs the federal government to strengthen diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility in the federal workforce. It creates government-wide and agency plans, reporting, and guidance to improve recruitment, hiring, promotion, retention, training, accommodations, and workplace culture. It also asks agencies to assess their current workforce practices and identify barriers and gaps.

14036.s: This order sets a policy to use antitrust laws and other agency powers to address overconcentration, monopolization, and unfair competition in the American economy. It directs agencies with overlapping authority to cooperate on investigations, mergers, and remedies, and it tells them to consider pro-competition regulations and to remove unnecessary barriers to entry. It also creates a White House Competition Council to coordinate federal efforts and identify additional administrative or legislative changes.

14037.s: This executive order directs federal agencies to consider new rules for cleaner cars and trucks, including vehicle emissions and fuel economy standards. It sets a goal for 50 percent of new passenger cars and light trucks sold in 2030 to be zero-emission vehicles. It also calls for coordination with state governments and other stakeholders while the rules are being considered.

14038.s: This order expands the national emergency related to Belarus and blocks property and property interests of certain people and entities linked to the Belarus government. It covers people involved in the government, certain sectors of the Belarus economy, and people tied to actions that threaten peace, human rights, election fairness, sanctions evasion, or public corruption. It also suspends the entry of noncitizens who meet these criteria, unless an official decides their entry is allowed.

14039.s: This order blocks property and property interests in the United States of certain foreign persons identified in a report to Congress about Russian energy export pipelines. It bars those persons from having their property transferred, paid, exported, withdrawn, or otherwise dealt in. The order also limits contributions of funds, goods, or services to or from those persons and directs agencies to carry out visa, admission, and parole restrictions under the law.

14040.s: This order directs the Attorney General and certain agency heads to review and declassify some records about the September 11 attacks. It covers FBI records from the PENTTBOM investigation, the subfile investigation, and other related records. The order also requires reports to the President and congressional intelligence committees, and public release of records that are declassified unless disclosure would materially impair confidential executive branch deliberations.

14041.s: This order creates a White House Initiative in the Department of Education to support Historically Black Colleges and Universities. It directs the Initiative to advise the President, coordinate federal efforts, and help HBCUs access federal programs, resources, grants, and procurement opportunities. It also creates a President’s Board of Advisors on HBCUs and requires federal agencies to submit yearly plans on efforts to strengthen HBCUs. The order revokes Executive Order 13779.

14042.s: This order requires many federal contractors and subcontractors to follow COVID-19 workplace safety guidance for workers on or connected to federal contracts. It applies to certain new contracts, contract-like instruments, renewals, extensions, and option exercises, and it excludes grants, some tribal agreements, small contracts, workers outside the United States, and subcontracts only for products. Agencies must add the required clause to covered contracts, and the order does not override more protective state or federal safety rules.

14043.s: This order requires federal agencies to run a program that makes COVID-19 vaccination mandatory for all federal employees, except where the law requires an exception. It also directs the Safer Federal Workforce Task Force to give guidance on how agencies should carry out the requirement. The order applies to federal employees and agencies covered by it.

14044.s: This order changes Executive Order 14007 to say the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology may have no more than 32 members. It affects the size of that council. The order also says it must be carried out under existing law and available funding.

14045.s: This order creates a White House Initiative in the Department of Education to advance educational equity and economic opportunity for Hispanic and Latino students, families, and communities. It sets policy goals that include improving early childhood access, reducing discriminatory discipline, improving data collection, supporting teachers and school leaders, and increasing access to college, career training, and work-based learning. It also directs federal agencies to form an interagency working group and prepare plans with measurable actions to support these goals.

14046.s: This order declares a national emergency over the crisis in northern Ethiopia. It lets the Treasury Secretary impose sanctions on foreign persons linked to actions that threaten peace, involve serious human rights abuse, block humanitarian aid, attack civilians, or undermine Ethiopia’s democratic process or territorial integrity. The order can block property, limit loans, restrict foreign exchange transactions, and deny visas or entry to certain noncitizens.

14047.s: This order adds measles to the list of quarantinable communicable diseases. It changes a prior executive order by placing measles on that list after infectious tuberculosis. It applies to the federal rules that cover quarantinable communicable diseases and must be carried out under applicable law.

14048.s: This order continues or reestablishes a list of federal advisory committees until September 30, 2023. It also changes the duties, membership terms, and leadership rules for some of those committees. The order assigns responsibility for those committees’ functions to the named department or agency heads under Federal Advisory Committee Act rules.

14049.s: This order creates a White House initiative in the Department of Education to help advance educational equity, excellence, and economic opportunity for Native American students. It directs federal agencies to work with Tribal Nations, Alaska Native entities, and Tribal Colleges and Universities. The initiative will focus on early childhood, K-12, higher education, Native language and cultural needs, career training, and better data on educational gaps.

14050.s: This order creates a White House initiative in the Department of Education to advance educational equity, excellence, and economic opportunity for Black Americans. It is aimed at Black students, families, and communities from early childhood through their chosen career. The order also sets up an interagency working group and requires agencies to prepare plans to help carry out the initiative's goals.

14051.s: This order designates the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment to release strategic and critical materials from the National Defense Stockpile. Those materials may be released for use, sale, or other disposition only when needed for national defense. The order does not allow releases for economic or budgetary purposes, and the Under Secretary must consult with relevant executive departments and agencies before ordering a release.

14052.s: This order directs federal agencies to help carry out the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. It says they should focus on efficient spending, stronger U.S. manufacturing and supply chains, job opportunities, equitable investment, resilient infrastructure, and work with State, local, Tribal, and territorial governments. It also creates an Infrastructure Implementation Task Force and a White House Infrastructure Coordinator to help coordinate these efforts.

14053.s: This order directs federal agencies to work with Tribal Nations to improve public safety and criminal justice for Native Americans and to respond to missing or murdered indigenous people. It calls for a coordinated law enforcement strategy, better data collection and information sharing, and more training and support for Tribal, State, local, and Federal law enforcement. It also directs plans to expand prevention, early intervention, and victim and survivor services, including mental health, substance abuse, child abuse reporting, and access to child advocacy center services.

14054.s: This order ends the national emergency tied to the situation in Burundi and revokes the earlier order that had been issued about it. It also ends the suspension of entry for certain immigrants and nonimmigrants covered by that earlier order. The order says this does not affect actions already taken, pending cases, or rights, duties, or penalties that had already accrued.

14055.s: This order directs federal agencies to include a clause in certain service contracts that gives qualified workers from the old contract a right of first refusal for jobs on the new contract. It also lets agencies consider keeping the work in the same locality when that is needed for economical and efficient service. The order does not apply to some small contracts or certain mixed federal and nonfederal jobs, and it sets rules for exceptions and enforcement.

14056.s: This order sets up the National Space Council and names its members, led by the Vice President. The Council advises the President on national space policy and strategy, coordinates space policy across agencies, and helps settle differences among agencies. It also creates a Users' Advisory Group of non-Federal representatives from aeronautical and space activities to give advice to the Council.

14057.s: This order directs federal agencies to lead on sustainability and climate adaptation. It sets goals for clean electricity, zero-emission vehicles, net-zero buildings, lower greenhouse gas emissions, less waste, and more sustainable buying. It also calls for tracking supplier emissions, expanding Buy Clean policies, and training the federal workforce. It affects federal agencies, federal workers, federal suppliers, and federal procurement.

14058.s: This order tells federal agencies to improve how they deliver services to the public and to make those services easier to use, more accessible, and more efficient. It directs several agencies to update online tools, forms, and customer support for things like passports, taxes, permits, nutrition benefits, workers' compensation, health care, education aid, veterans services, airport security, and disaster assistance. It also says agencies should reduce paperwork and administrative burdens while protecting civil rights, privacy, confidentiality, and information security.

14059.s: This order declares a national emergency over the international trafficking of illicit drugs, including fentanyl and other synthetic opioids. It authorizes sanctions against foreign persons who help produce, sell, finance, transport, or support illicit drugs or their means of production. It can block property, limit financial transactions, bar certain investments, and suspend the entry of some noncitizens into the United States.

14060.s: This executive order creates a United States Council on Transnational Organized Crime to coordinate federal efforts against transnational criminal organizations. It also creates a Strategic Division at the Department of Justice to produce strategic plans and support the council. The order calls for agencies to share information, provide personnel and resources, and improve efforts against illicit finance and other transnational crime.

14061.s: This order sets new basic pay rates and salaries for several federal pay systems, including the General Schedule, Foreign Service, Veterans Health Administration, Senior Executive Service, Executive Schedule, Vice President, Congress, justices and judges, uniformed services, and administrative law judges. It also provides locality-based comparability payments. The changes take effect on January 1, 2022, or at the start of the first applicable pay period after that date, and it supersedes Executive Order 13970 on those effective dates.

14062.s: This order amends Parts II and IV of the Manual for Courts-Martial, United States. The changes take effect on the date of the order and apply to military justice matters under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. It does not make punishable any act that was not punishable when done, and it does not invalidate certain actions that began before the order.

14063.s: This order directs federal agencies to use project labor agreements on large-scale federal construction projects. It says contractors and subcontractors on those projects must agree to negotiate or join a project labor agreement, unless an agency grants an exception. The order also sets requirements for those agreements, including dispute resolution and protections against strikes and lockouts. Agencies must report their use of project labor agreements and the exceptions they grant.

14064.s: This order blocks certain property and interests in property of Da Afghanistan Bank that are held in the United States by U.S. financial institutions. Those institutions must transfer the blocked property into a consolidated account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. It also prohibits transactions or conspiracies that try to evade or violate these restrictions.

14065.s: This order blocks property and interests in property of certain people tied to operations in the covered regions of Ukraine. It also bans new investment there and bars imports from, and exports to, those regions. The order suspends the entry of certain noncitizens who meet the listed criteria, unless an official decides their entry is not against U.S. interests.

14066.s: This order expands the national emergency over Russia’s war against Ukraine. It prohibits imports into the United States of Russian crude oil, petroleum, liquefied natural gas, coal, and related products. It also prohibits new investment in the energy sector in the Russian Federation by United States persons and blocks certain support for foreign transactions that would be banned if done by a U.S. person.

14067.s: This order says the United States should develop digital assets in a responsible way and protect consumers, investors, businesses, financial stability, national security, privacy, and access to financial services. It directs federal officials to coordinate actions on digital assets and central bank digital currencies. The Secretary of the Treasury must submit a report on the future of money and payment systems, including possible effects on the U.S. financial system, economic growth, financial inclusion, and national security.

14068.s: This order prohibits imports of certain products from the Russian Federation, including fish, seafood, alcoholic beverages, and non-industrial diamonds. It also bans the export, reexport, sale, or supply of luxury goods and U.S. dollar-denominated banknotes to the Russian Federation or people there. It bars new investment in any sector of the Russian Federation economy that is determined under the order, and it prohibits transactions that evade these rules or conspire to violate them.

14069.s: This order directs federal officials to consider new rules for federal procurement that would promote pay equity and transparency. It says they should look at whether federal contractors and subcontractors should be limited or barred from asking about or using job applicants' and employees' current or past pay when making employment decisions. It also says they should consider accountability measures for any new rules.

14070.s: This order directs federal agencies to review their health coverage policies and look for ways to expand affordable coverage, improve coverage quality, strengthen benefits, and help more Americans enroll. It focuses on Medicaid, Medicare, the ACA Marketplaces, and other health programs. It also tells agencies to look at ways to make enrollment and coverage easier and to reduce the burden of medical debt on households.

14071.s: This order prohibits new investment in the Russian Federation by United States persons. It also prohibits certain services from the United States, or by United States persons, to people in the Russian Federation, as determined by the Secretary of the Treasury with the Secretary of State. It also bars actions that help evade these bans, and it does not stop official business for the Federal Government or the United Nations.

14072.s: This order directs federal agencies to conserve and restore mature and old-growth forests on federal lands, reduce wildfire risk, and support climate-smart forestry and reforestation. It requires an inventory of old-growth and mature forests, and it calls for policies on forest conservation, wildfire mitigation, and reforestation targets. It also asks for reports on stopping international deforestation and on ways to use nature-based solutions across the federal government. It affects federal land managers, other agencies, and coordination with state, Tribal, local, private, and nonprofit partners.

14073.s: This order creates the National Quantum Initiative Advisory Committee and tells it to advise the President and two White House subcommittees on the National Quantum Initiative Program. The committee is made up of the Office of Science and Technology Policy Director or designee and up to 26 presidential appointees from industry, universities, and federal laboratories. It must meet at least twice a year, review the national strategy for quantum information science, and respond to requests for information and advice. The order also revokes a 2019 executive order that had established the committee.

14074.s: This order directs federal agencies to improve policing and criminal justice practices, with a focus on public trust, fairness, transparency, and accountability. It calls for better investigations of deaths in custody and civil rights violations, along with changes to recruitment, hiring, promotion, training, and discipline in law enforcement. It also addresses conditions for incarcerated people, their access to health care and rehabilitation, and full implementation of the First Step Act. State, Tribal, local, and territorial law enforcement agencies may also receive guidance and support under the order.

14075.s: This order directs federal agencies to act against discrimination and barriers facing lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and intersex individuals and families. It requires actions on health care, education, child welfare, housing, and family support, including steps related to LGBTQI+ youth, older adults, and people facing homelessness. It also tells agencies to study federal benefit eligibility, issue guidance, and develop reports and sample policies for states, schools, and other programs.

14076.s: This order directs federal agencies to take steps to protect access to reproductive healthcare services, including abortion. It also calls for actions to expand outreach and education, protect patient privacy and security, and address deceptive or fraudulent practices. The order applies to federal agencies, healthcare providers, patients, and others seeking or providing these services.

14077.s: This order sets up an emergency board to investigate disputes between certain railroads and their employees represented by certain labor organizations. The board has a chair and two other members appointed by the President and must report to the President within 30 days. During that time, and for 30 days after the report is submitted, the parties may not change the conditions that led to the disputes unless they agree to do so.

14078.s: This order says the United States will keep using existing hostage recovery rules and adds new steps for people held hostage or wrongfully detained abroad. It directs government offices to coordinate on finding options, sharing information, and helping the families and return of affected United States nationals. It also allows the government to block property of foreign persons tied to hostage-taking or wrongful detention and to suspend the entry of certain noncitizens into the United States.

14079.s: This order directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to consider actions to improve access to reproductive healthcare services, including through Medicaid for patients traveling across state lines for medical care. It also directs HHS to work on compliance with federal non-discrimination laws so people are not denied needed healthcare based on pregnancy or related conditions. The order calls for a review of research and data collection on the effect of access to reproductive healthcare on maternal health and other health outcomes.

14080.s: This executive order directs federal agencies to help carry out the CHIPS Act of 2022. It says agencies should protect taxpayer resources, build domestic semiconductor manufacturing, support private investment, and strengthen research and innovation. It also creates a CHIPS Implementation Steering Council to coordinate this work across the executive branch.

14081.s: This order directs the federal government to coordinate efforts to advance biotechnology and biomanufacturing for health, climate change, energy, food security, agriculture, supply chains, and national and economic security. It calls for reports, an implementation plan, and a data initiative to support research, production, and the use of biological data. It also directs agencies to address biosafety, biosecurity, privacy, security risks, and ethical issues, and to consult outside stakeholders.

14082.s: This order directs federal agencies to help carry out the energy and infrastructure parts of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. It says agencies should focus on clean energy, lower energy costs, energy security, climate goals, environmental justice, jobs, and better coordination with state, local, Tribal, territorial, and private partners. It also creates a White House Office on Clean Energy Innovation and Implementation and changes other executive orders to support this work.

14083.s: This order directs the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States to give more attention to national security risks from foreign investments. It says the committee should consider effects on supply chains, technology leadership, and cybersecurity, including access to sensitive data and critical infrastructure. It also says the committee may look at patterns of related investments over time and how foreign ties could affect a transaction.

14084.s: This executive order says the Administration will promote the arts, the humanities, and museum and library services. It directs federal agencies to coordinate with the heads of the NEA, NEH, and IMLS on projects that support these goals. It also creates the President's Committee on the Arts and the Humanities to give advice on these issues.

14085.s: This order changes rules for several military decorations and awards. It updates the Air Medal, Good Conduct Medal, Bronze Star Medal, and Defense Distinguished Service Medal, and it also changes how certain unit citations and award approvals are handled. The changes apply to members of the Armed Forces, including the Space Force and, in one case, the Coast Guard and Homeland Security.

14087.s: This order directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to consider new payment and delivery models to lower drug costs and improve access to innovative drug therapies for people in Medicare and Medicaid. It says these models may lead to lower cost-sharing for commonly used drugs and support value-based payment. The Secretary must also report on any selected models and then take steps to test them.

14088.s: This order adds steps under the national emergency related to Nicaragua. It expands who can be targeted, including people involved in arresting or prosecuting someone mainly for freedom of expression or assembly, and it updates rules for blocking property. It also allows bans on some Nicaraguan imports, certain exports and sales to people in Nicaragua, new investment in parts of Nicaragua's economy, and some financing or guarantees by U.S. persons.

14089.s: This order creates a President's Advisory Council on African Diaspora Engagement within the Department of State. The council must advise the President on strengthening connections between the U.S. government and the African Diaspora in the United States. It is made up of up to 12 members from African American and African immigrant communities, and the State Department must provide funding and administrative support when allowed by law.

14090.s: This order sets new basic pay and salary rates for several federal pay systems, including the General Schedule, Foreign Service, Veterans Health Administration, Senior Executive Service, Executive Schedule, Congress, justices and judges, uniformed services, and administrative law judges. It also provides locality-based comparability payments and directs the Office of Personnel Management to take actions needed to carry them out. The new rates take effect on the dates listed in the order, and it supersedes Executive Order 14061 on those dates.

14091.s: This order tells federal agencies to keep working on racial equity and support for underserved communities across government programs and services. It creates Agency Equity Teams in several agencies and a White House Steering Committee on Equity to coordinate these efforts and track progress. Agencies must also submit public Equity Action Plans each year with actions and performance measures to advance equity.

14092.s: This order directs federal agencies to take actions to reduce gun violence and improve public safety. It requires reports on how the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act is being carried out and asks for plans on firearms background checks, safe storage, extreme risk protection orders, and support for survivors and communities affected by gun violence. It also directs steps on firearms dealer compliance, ballistics data reporting, firearm shipment losses or thefts, and military and civilian marketing of firearms.

14093.s: This order says executive departments and agencies may not make operational use of commercial spyware if it poses significant counterintelligence or security risks to the United States Government or significant risks of improper use by a foreign government or foreign person. It also bars agencies from asking or directly enabling a third party to make that kind of use. Agencies must review existing uses, create internal controls and oversight, and share relevant information with the Director of National Intelligence and the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs.

14094.s: This order updates how federal agencies review regulations. It says agencies should seek input from affected communities, the public, businesses, workers, and other interested parties, and it changes how meetings and public comments are handled in the review process. It also directs officials to update regulatory analysis guidance to recognize distributive impacts and equity when allowed by law.

14095.s: This order tells federal agencies to work on increasing access to affordable, high-quality child care and long-term care, and to support family caregivers. It directs agencies to look at ways to improve pay, benefits, training, staffing, and working conditions for care workers, including early educators and long-term care workers. It also calls for steps to help family caregivers through health care programs, veterans programs, and Medicare information access.

14096.s: This order directs federal agencies to make environmental justice part of their work. It says agencies should identify and address disproportionate harm to communities with environmental justice concerns, including harms related to climate change, pollution, and other environmental burdens. It also requires agencies to provide meaningful public participation, improve access for people with limited English or disabilities, and continue consultation with Tribal Nations on federal actions that affect them.

14097.s: This order gives the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of Homeland Security added authority to respond to the national emergency tied to international drug trafficking. It lets the Secretaries of the Army, Navy, and Air Force, and the Secretary of Homeland Security for the Coast Guard in some cases, order Ready Reserve units and members to active duty when they consider it necessary. It applies only under the terms of the law it cites and depends on available appropriations.

14098.s: This order blocks property and property interests of certain foreign persons tied to actions that threaten Sudan’s peace, security, or democratic transition. It also bars support to those persons and can suspend their entry into the United States as immigrants or nonimmigrants. The order also covers people who help, control, or are closely connected to blocked persons, and it restricts donations and transactions that would evade these limits.

14099.s: This order revokes the COVID-19 vaccination requirement for federal employees and the COVID-19 safety protocols for federal contractors. Agency policies based on those orders may no longer be enforced and must be rescinded under applicable law. The order applies to federal agencies, federal employees, and federal contractors and subcontractors.

14100.s: This order directs federal agencies to improve hiring and retention for military and veteran spouses, military caregivers, and survivors. It calls for a government-wide plan, yearly training for hiring staff, better data tracking, and reports on these groups in federal employment. It also directs agencies to consider telework, remote work, and up to 5 days of administrative leave for military spouses during certain relocations, and to examine ways to reduce barriers to jobs, training, and benefits for these families.

14101.s: This order directs federal agencies to take steps to improve access to affordable contraception and family planning services. It calls for possible guidance under the Affordable Care Act, Medicaid, Medicare, and other federal health programs to expand coverage, lower out-of-pocket costs, and improve access to information and care. It also asks agencies to support training, technical assistance, privacy protections, and research on gaps in access. These actions affect women, patients, health providers, federal program participants, and people covered by federal health programs.

14102.s: This order lets the Secretary of Defense, and the Secretary of Homeland Security for the Coast Guard in some cases, order some Selected Reserve units and certain Individual Ready Reserve members to active duty. It says this is to help support Operation Atlantic Resolve in and around the U.S. European Command area. No more than 3,000 members can be on active duty under this order at one time, and no more than 450 may be from the Individual Ready Reserve.

14103.s: This order amends parts of the Manual for Courts-Martial, United States, and adds new appendices. The changes apply to military justice rules and procedures under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. Some amendments take effect on the date of the order, others follow later effective dates set in the order or in the NDAA FY 2022.

14104.s: This order tells federal agencies to consider domestic manufacturing when they fund research and development. It says new technologies developed with support from the U.S. government should be made in the United States whenever possible and allowed by law. It also requires agencies to track and report where subject inventions are made and used, and to review waivers of domestic manufacturing rules.

14106.s: This order directs the Secretary of Homeland Security to carry out certain Coast Guard officer personnel functions that are normally vested in the President. Those functions include approving or changing selection board reports, appointing and removing officers, making temporary appointments, and approving some continuation and warrant officer actions. During a time of war or national emergency, it also allows the Secretary to suspend some laws on Coast Guard officer selection, promotion, and separation, and on Coast Guard Reserve officers.

14107.s: This order exempts Paul H. Maurer, the current Special Agent in Charge of the George W. Bush Protective Detail in Dallas, Texas, from automatic separation under federal law. The Director of the United States Secret Service keeps all applicable supervisory authority over him, and the order says it creates no enforceable right or benefit against the United States.

14108.s: This order directs federal agencies to keep responding to the East Palestine train derailment and to use their authority and resources to support recovery. It requires a federal disaster recovery coordinator to assess unmet needs in the affected communities and look for needs that may qualify for federal assistance. It also keeps EPA cleanup, air and water monitoring, and HHS public health monitoring going, and asks DOT, EPA, and HHS for reports on their work.

14109.s: This order continues a list of federal advisory committees until September 30, 2025. The committees include ones on science, labor, health, homeland security, veterans small business development, environmental issues, and several national monuments. It also changes two earlier executive orders, including ones about Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians, and Pacific Islanders, and about the arts, humanities, and museum and library services.

14110.s: This order sets a federal policy for the safe, secure, and trustworthy development and use of artificial intelligence. It directs agencies to focus on safety testing, consumer protections, privacy, civil rights, worker protections, and responsible innovation. It also calls for better labeling of AI-generated content, stronger government AI oversight, and cooperation with international partners on AI risks and safeguards.

14111.s: This order creates the Interagency Security Committee to set policies and standards for security in Federal facilities. It covers buildings and facilities in the United States used by Federal employees or Federal contractor workers for nonmilitary activities. The committee also reviews existing security standards, monitors compliance, and can form working groups to help carry out its work.

14112.s: This order tells federal agencies to work with the White House Council on Native American Affairs to improve how federal funding and support programs for Tribal Nations are run. It directs agencies to look for funding shortfalls, report needed changes, and recommend budget, law, or rule changes to better meet the needs of Tribal Nations. It also tells agencies to reduce paperwork and other burdens, and to make funding more flexible and easier for Tribal Nations to access.

14113.s: This order sets new basic pay rates for several federal pay systems, including the General Schedule, Foreign Service, Veterans Health Administration, Senior Executive Service, the Executive Schedule, Congress, justices and judges, uniformed services, and administrative law judges. It also directs locality-based comparability payments and tells the Office of Personnel Management to take steps to carry them out. The pay schedules take effect on January 1, 2024, or on the first applicable pay period after that date.

14114.s: This order expands sanctions on foreign financial institutions that make significant transactions for people tied to Russia’s technology, defense, construction, aerospace, or manufacturing sectors, or that help Russia’s military-industrial base. It also allows the blocking of property and restrictions on correspondent or payable-through accounts in the United States for those institutions. The order adds import limits on certain products of Russian origin, including fish, seafood, alcoholic beverages, non-industrial diamonds, and other products the government may determine. It directs federal agencies to issue rules and carry out these measures.

14115.s: This order blocks property and property interests of certain foreign persons tied to actions that threaten the peace, security, or stability of the West Bank. It covers people involved in violence against civilians, forced displacement, property destruction, seizure of property, support for blocked persons, or acts of terrorism affecting the West Bank. It also suspends the immigrant and nonimmigrant entry of noncitizens who meet these criteria, unless the Secretary of State or the Secretary of Homeland Security decides their entry is not contrary to U.S. interests.

14116.s: This order changes Coast Guard rules for protecting vessels, harbors, ports, and waterfront facilities. It adds rules covering digital infrastructure and cyber incidents, and gives the Captain of the Port more authority to set security zones, inspect and search vessels and facilities, control movement, and remove people or items not allowed. It also requires immediate reporting of sabotage or a cyber incident to the FBI, CISA, and the Captain of the Port, and says masters, owners, operators, and agents remain responsible for protection and security.

14117.s: This order directs federal agencies to create rules that restrict certain U.S. transactions involving Americans' bulk sensitive personal data and United States Government-related data when a country of concern could gain access. It covers acquisitions, transfers, exports, and other dealings in property tied to a foreign country or national, unless an exception or license applies. The order also directs the Attorney General and the Secretary of Homeland Security to identify prohibited and restricted transactions, countries of concern, and security requirements.

14118.s: This order ends the national emergency declared over actions and policies of certain members of the Government of Zimbabwe and other persons. It also revokes Executive Orders 13288, 13391, and 13469. The order says it does not affect actions already taken, pending proceedings, or rights, duties, or penalties that already matured or were incurred.

14119.s: This order directs federal agencies to expand the use of Registered Apprenticeships in hiring, training, and career development. It also tells agencies to review grants and procurement for ways to require, score, or encourage grantees and contractors to use Registered Apprenticeships or Pre-Apprenticeships. The order revokes a previous order on Labor-Management Forums and tells covered agencies to create or use forums where managers, employees, and union representatives can discuss workplace issues and federal operations.

14120.s: This order directs federal agencies to advance women’s health research and close gaps in research and data. It tells agencies to look at research standards, funding, clinical trials, and ways to improve the study of conditions that affect women differently or disproportionately. It also calls for new work on menopause and midlife health, including for women service members and veterans.

14121.s: This executive order directs the Secretary of the Interior to review sites of national importance tied to women’s history and look for ways to highlight important figures and chapters in that history. It also directs an overview theme study on women’s history, followed by additional theme studies, and asks for recommendations on improving how women’s history is recognized across Federal parks, lands, and programs. The findings must also be made available to the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum and its council for possible use in exhibits.

14122.s: This order keeps the Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy in a central role for pandemic preparedness and response. It transfers some COVID-19 response duties to the office’s director and ends the COVID-19 Response Coordinator and Deputy Coordinator positions. It also revokes three earlier executive orders about hoarding medical resources, mask-wearing for the federal workforce, and COVID-19 safety in travel.

14123.s:
This order keeps and strengthens the White House Council on Supply Chain Resilience. The council is led by the National Security Affairs and Economic Policy advisers and includes cabinet officials and other federal leaders.

It directs the council to coordinate federal work on supply chain resilience and industrial competitiveness, identify supply chain risks, and work with allies and partners. It also requires the council to review industries critical to national or economic security and report to the President, with recommendations on supply chains, trade, workforce issues, and support for small businesses and family-owned farming operations.

14124.s: This order creates a White House Initiative in the Department of Education to support Hispanic-Serving Institutions. It directs the initiative to help these schools get access to federal programs and resources, share best practices, and improve student success and economic mobility. It also creates a President's Board of Advisors on Hispanic-Serving Institutions to advise the President on these goals. The order affects Hispanic-Serving Institutions and the students, faculty, staff, and communities they serve.

14125.s: This order creates an emergency board to investigate a dispute between New Jersey Transit Rail Operations and its locomotive engineers represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen. The board will report to the President within 30 days. For 120 days after the board is created, the parties may not change the conditions that led to the dispute unless they agree to do so.

14126.s: This order directs federal agencies to give preference to projects that support good jobs, worker safety, fair pay, and worker access to union representation when they select projects for federal financial assistance. It says agencies should consider labor agreements, benefits like paid leave and health care, training and apprenticeship programs, and steps to reduce discrimination and help workers from underserved communities. It also creates a task force to help carry out the order across several federal departments and agencies.

14127.s: This order creates an interagency task force to coordinate work on emerging firearms threats, including machinegun conversion devices, 3D printed firearms, and undetectable firearms. It requires the task force to study how these items are used, where they come from, and what legal tools agencies have to stop them, including import and export laws. It also tells agencies to work together on school safety and to help schools design and conduct active-shooter drills that are effective and appropriate for students' ages and development.

14128.s: This order establishes a second emergency board to investigate and report on a dispute between New Jersey Transit Rail Operations and its locomotive engineers represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen. The board is made up of a chair and two other members appointed by the President. The parties must submit final offers within 30 days after the board is created, and the board must then report to the President within 30 days after those offers are submitted. From the request to create the board until 60 days after the report is submitted, the parties must not change the conditions out of which the dispute arose unless they agree to do so.

14129.s: This order closes all executive departments and agencies of the Federal Government on December 24, 2024, and excuses their employees from duty that day. Agency heads may keep some offices open and require some employees to report for national security, defense, or other public need. It also says December 24, 2024, will be treated under federal pay and leave rules.

14130.s: This order amends parts of the Manual for Courts-Martial, United States. It also sets rules for the randomized selection of qualified personnel to serve as court-martial members to the maximum extent practicable. The changes take effect on the dates listed in the order, and cases or actions already started may continue under the old rules.

14131.s: This order updates rules for the Presidential Service Certificate and Presidential Service Badge for members of the United States Uniformed Services who serve in the White House Office, White House Military Office support units, or other direct support jobs in the Executive Office of the President. It also updates the Vice Presidential Service Badge for members assigned to duty in the Office of the Vice President or related support duties. The order says when these badges and certificates may be awarded, who may award them, and when they may be worn on a uniform.

14132.s: This order sets new basic pay rates and salaries for several federal pay systems, including the General Schedule, Foreign Service, Veterans Health Administration, Senior Executive Service, and administrative law judges. It also sets pay for certain executive, legislative, and judicial offices, and for members of the uniformed services and cadets or midshipmen. The order directs that locality-based comparability payments be paid under the listed schedule. Most of the schedules take effect with the first applicable pay period beginning on or after January 1, 2025, and Schedule 8 takes effect on January 1, 2025.

14133.s: This order closes all executive departments and agencies of the federal government on January 9, 2025, as a mark of respect for James Earl Carter, Jr. Agency heads may keep some offices or employees open on that day for national security, defense, or other public need. It also says that day counts under certain pay and leave rules for federal employees.

14134.s: This order sets the line of succession for the Secretary of Agriculture if both the Secretary and Deputy Secretary cannot serve. It lists Department of Agriculture officials who would act as Secretary in a set order, with some limits for people already serving in an acting role or not otherwise eligible under the law. It also revokes the prior Agriculture succession order from 2012.

14135.s: This order sets the line of succession for the Secretary of Homeland Security if the Secretary, Deputy Secretary, Under Secretary for Management, and certain other officers cannot do the job. It lists four officials who would act as Secretary in the order named, unless they are serving in an acting role or are not eligible under the law. It also revokes a prior order on Homeland Security succession and removes one section from another order.

14136.s: This order sets a list of Department of Justice officials who would act as Attorney General if the Attorney General, Deputy Attorney General, Associate Attorney General, and certain other designated officers cannot serve. It names the United States Attorneys for the Southern District of New York, the District of Arizona, the Northern District of Illinois, and the District of Hawaii in that order. It also says certain acting officials and others who are not otherwise eligible cannot serve under this order, and it revokes a prior order on DOJ succession.

14137.s: This order sets the line of succession for who will act as Secretary of the Treasury if both the Secretary and the Deputy Secretary are unable to serve. It lists Treasury officials in order, starting with Under Secretaries and then other named offices. It also says people serving in those offices in an acting capacity do not automatically become acting Secretary, and it revokes a 2016 order on Treasury succession.

14138.s: This order sets a list of Office of Management and Budget officials who will act as Director if both the Director and Deputy Director cannot perform their duties. It says people serving in those jobs in an acting capacity, or those not otherwise eligible under the law, may not act as Director under this order. It also revokes a 2012 executive order with a similar succession rule.

14139.s: This order sets the line of succession for the Office of the National Cyber Director if the Director dies, resigns, or cannot do the job. It lists which officials would act as Director, in order, starting with the Deputy National Cyber Director and ending with the General Counsel. It also says no one serving in an acting role can use this order to become Director, and the President may depart from the order if allowed by law.

14140.s: This order expands sanctions related to the Western Balkans. It blocks property and interests in property of certain people in the United States or under control of U.S. persons if the Treasury Secretary, with the Secretary of State, determines they threatened peace, security, stability, territorial integrity, democratic processes, or certain agreements in the region. It also covers people involved in serious human rights abuse, corruption, support for blocked persons, and some spouses or adult children of blocked persons.

14141.s: This order directs the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of Energy to identify federal sites that may be leased to non-Federal entities for frontier AI data centers and clean energy facilities. It says AI infrastructure in the United States should support national security, economic competitiveness, and clean power. It also says development should not raise energy costs for consumers and businesses, and should include strong labor standards and community consultation.
