14142.s: This order changes a previous Syria emergency order. It removes one reference to the Government of Turkey’s military offensive into northeast Syria. It also changes the rules on who can be blocked under that order, including people or groups that help, fund, supply, or act for someone whose property is blocked.

14143.s: This order lets certain AmeriCorps alumni be appointed noncompetitively to competitive service jobs in the Federal Government if they are qualified and certified by AmeriCorps. It applies to people who completed certain national service terms of at least 1,700 hours. It does not change the rules for VISTA members who successfully complete their service.

14144.s: This order directs federal agencies to strengthen cybersecurity by improving software supply chain security, cloud security, identity management, and threat hunting across federal networks. It requires new steps for software providers to attest to secure development practices, and it calls for updated federal standards and guidance on secure software delivery, patches, and open source software. It also directs agencies to use phishing-resistant authentication in pilots or larger deployments and to improve CISA’s access to agency data to identify cyber threats and coordinated attacks.

14145.s: This order tells federal agencies to coordinate programs that help left-behind communities, including covered communities in economically distressed regions, Tribal lands, rural communities, and disaster recovery areas. It directs agencies to improve outreach, technical assistance, and access to federal grants, and to give preference in some funding opportunities to applications from entities in and serving covered communities. It also calls for support after disasters for long-term economic development, infrastructure needs, and help with the application process.

14146.s: This order revokes Sections 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7 of Executive Order 13961. It also renumbers the remaining sections and changes two references in that order. The changes affect the rules for federal mission resilience and the committees named in that earlier order.

14147.s: This order tells the Attorney General to review civil and criminal enforcement actions by federal departments and agencies over the last 4 years and report any conduct that may have gone against the order’s purpose. It also tells the Director of National Intelligence to review the Intelligence Community’s actions over the last 4 years and send a report with recommendations for remedial action. Departments and agencies must follow document-retention rules, and any noncompliance must be referred to the Attorney General.

14148.s: This order revokes many previous executive orders and presidential memoranda. Those revoked actions cover DEI policies, immigration, climate, health care, COVID-19, voting, education, and other federal programs and directives. It also directs agency heads and White House officials to review related federal actions and recommend or make further changes.

14149.s: This order tells federal departments, agencies, officers, employees, and agents not to act or use federal resources in a way that would unlawfully limit protected speech. It also directs the Attorney General to investigate federal government activities over the last 4 years that were inconsistent with this order and to prepare a report with recommended corrective actions.

14150.s: This order directs the Secretary of State to issue guidance to align the State Department’s policies, programs, personnel, and operations with an America First foreign policy. It says U.S. foreign policy should put America and American citizens first. It applies to the Department of State and is to be carried out under existing law and available funding.

14151.s: This order directs federal agencies to end all discriminatory DEI and DEIA programs, policies, preferences, and activities in the federal government. It also requires agencies to review and revise federal employment practices, union contracts, and training policies so they do not consider DEI or DEIA factors. Agencies must also work to terminate DEI, DEIA, and environmental justice offices, positions, plans, grants, contracts, and employee performance requirements where allowed by law.

14153.s: This order directs federal agencies to speed up the development of Alaska’s natural resources, including energy, minerals, timber, seafood, and LNG. It also tells agencies to review, revoke, or replace a number of Alaska-related rules, plans, leases, and decisions on federal and state lands. The order affects agencies handling land use, permits, roads, waterways, hunting and fishing, and Alaska Native land issues in Alaska.

14154.s: This order directs federal agencies to encourage energy exploration and production on federal lands and waters, promote the production and processing of non-fuel minerals, and remove rules the order says burden domestic energy development. It also directs agencies to review and suspend, revise, or rescind certain energy-related actions, and it revokes several earlier executive orders. The order calls for faster permitting, changes to environmental reviews, and a pause on disbursement of some funds appropriated through the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 and the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

14156.s: This order declares a national emergency over the United States' energy supply and grid. It tells federal agencies to use lawful emergency authorities to speed up the identification, leasing, production, transportation, refining, and generation of domestic energy resources. It also directs agencies to use emergency permitting rules and to report actions taken under the order.

14157.s: This order creates a process to designate certain international cartels and other organizations as Foreign Terrorist Organizations or Specially Designated Global Terrorists. It says these groups pose a threat to the United States and directs the Secretary of State, Attorney General, and Secretary of Homeland Security to take steps to carry out the order. It also declares a national emergency to deal with those threats.

14158.s: This order creates the Department of Government Efficiency to modernize federal technology and software and to try to improve government efficiency and productivity. It renames the United States Digital Service as the United States DOGE Service and sets up a temporary organization within it that will end on July 4, 2026. It also requires each agency to create a DOGE Team of at least four employees and gives USDS access to unclassified agency records, software systems, and IT systems.

14159.s: This order tells federal agencies to enforce immigration laws against inadmissible and removable aliens, with a focus on public safety and national security. It revokes several prior immigration executive orders and directs agencies to review and revoke related policies. It also calls for more removals, more detention facilities, cooperation with state and local law enforcement, fines and penalties, and steps to encourage unlawful aliens to leave the United States.

14161.s: This order directs federal officials to increase screening and vetting of aliens seeking admission to the United States or already in the country. It also calls for identifying countries with poor vetting information that could justify a partial or full suspension of entry, and for taking steps to exclude or remove certain aliens when the information supports it. The order further tells officials to review visa programs, refugee and stateless admission safeguards, and other policies related to national security and public safety.

14162.s: This order directs the United States to withdraw from the Paris Agreement and from any other agreement, pact, accord, or similar commitment made under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. It also tells officials to stop or revoke any financial commitment made under that framework and revokes the U.S. International Climate Finance Plan. The order says future international energy agreements should prioritize economic efficiency, American prosperity, consumer choice, and fiscal restraint.

14163.s: This order suspends the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program until a later finding says resuming it is in the interests of the United States. It also pauses decisions on refugee status applications, with some case-by-case exceptions if officials decide an entry is in the national interest and not a threat to security or welfare. The order directs agencies to review whether state and local governments can have a greater role in refugee placement, and it revokes a 2021 executive order on refugee programs.

14164.s: This order directs the Attorney General to seek the death penalty for crimes that meet the standard for it, including every federal capital crime involving the murder of a law-enforcement officer or a capital crime committed by an alien illegally present in the country. It also directs the Attorney General to review the 37 murderers whose federal death sentences were commuted, look at their prison conditions, and consider whether they can be charged with state capital crimes. The order tells the Attorney General to help states keep enough lethal injection drugs, act on state certification requests, and seek the overruling of Supreme Court precedents that limit capital punishment.

14165.s: This order directs federal agencies to secure the southern border and stop the entry of illegal aliens into the United States. It calls for physical barriers, more personnel, detention of people apprehended for immigration violations, and the removal of people who enter or stay in violation of federal law. It also tells agencies to end certain parole practices, resume Migrant Protection Protocols, and increase cooperation with state, local, and international partners.

14166.s: This order tells the Attorney General not to enforce the Act against TikTok for 75 days. It also says the Justice Department must not take action or impose penalties for conduct during that period, or for conduct that happened before this order. The order covers TikTok and other apps operated directly or indirectly by ByteDance Ltd. or TikTok.

14167.s: This order directs the Armed Forces to prioritize protecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the United States along its national borders. It tells the Secretary of Defense to revise military planning so U.S. Northern Command can help seal the borders and repel unlawful mass migration, narcotics trafficking, human smuggling and trafficking, and other criminal activities. It also requires ongoing assessments of options to protect the United States from mass unlawful entry and threats to national sovereignty and security.

14168.s: This executive order says the federal government will recognize two sexes, male and female, and defines sex-based terms for federal policy. It directs agencies to use sex, not gender, in federal documents and forms, and to make government identification and personnel records reflect a person’s sex. It also orders agencies to remove policies and guidance that promote gender ideology, and to block federal funds from being used for that purpose.

14169.s: This order pauses new United States foreign development assistance funds for 90 days while those programs are reviewed for efficiency and consistency with United States foreign policy. It says department and agency heads must review foreign assistance programs and decide whether to continue, change, or stop them, with approval from the Secretary of State and the Director of OMB. New foreign assistance programs and obligations must be approved by the Secretary of State or his designee, in consultation with the Director of OMB. The Secretary of State may waive the pause for specific programs.

14170.s: This order directs the government to create a Federal Hiring Plan for federal agencies. The plan would focus on hiring skilled Americans, prevent hiring based on race, sex, or religion, and use more technical and alternative assessments. It also calls for faster hiring, better updates to candidates, and more use of technology in the hiring process.

14171.s: This order reinstates a prior policy for certain Federal jobs that are confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating. It says employees in or applying for those jobs do not have to personally or politically support the current President or administration, but they must faithfully implement administration policies or face dismissal. It directs the Office of Personnel Management to change civil service rules and issue guidance on more positions to consider, and it revokes Executive Order 14003.

14172.s: This order directs the Interior Secretary to restore the name "Mount McKinley" and update federal geographic records, while the park around it keeps the name Denali National Park and Preserve. It also directs that the Gulf of Mexico be renamed the "Gulf of America" in federal records and on federal maps, contracts, and other documents. The order tells the Interior Secretary and the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to take related actions and consider additional names to honor.

14173.s: This order tells executive departments and agencies to end discriminatory and illegal race- and sex-based preferences, policies, programs, and activities, including those tied to DEI and DEIA. It revokes several earlier executive orders and a presidential memorandum, and it changes federal contracting and grant rules to require compliance with federal anti-discrimination laws. It also directs agencies to review private-sector DEI practices, share enforcement recommendations, and give guidance to state and local education agencies and higher education institutions that receive federal funds.

14174.s: This order revokes two earlier executive orders. One of those orders required COVID safety protocols for federal contractors, and the other required coronavirus vaccination for federal employees. It affects federal contractors and federal employees.

14175.s: This order starts the process to consider Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, for designation as a Foreign Terrorist Organization. It directs the Secretary of State to report on the designation and then take appropriate action, and it would also require a review of certain USAID partners, nonprofits, and contractors in Yemen. If Ansar Allah is designated, USAID must review entities linked to it and may end projects, grants, or contracts as appropriate.

14177.s: This order creates the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. The council advises the President on science, technology, education, innovation policy, and scientific and technical information for public policy on the American economy, workers, and national and homeland security. It includes members from outside the federal government, can form subcommittees and ad hoc groups, and is set to end in 2 years unless the President extends it.

14178.s: This order says the administration will support the growth and use of digital assets, blockchain technology, and related technologies. It tells agencies not to establish, issue, or promote central bank digital currencies, except where required by law. It also ends Executive Order 14067 and creates a working group to review digital asset rules and make recommendations on future regulations and legislation.

14179.s: This order directs federal officials to develop an artificial intelligence action plan within 180 days. It also requires a review of policies and actions under the revoked Executive Order 14110 and allows agencies to suspend, revise, or rescind those actions if needed. The order says the United States should sustain and enhance its global AI dominance for human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security.

14180.s: This order creates a council to review the Federal Emergency Management Agency and advise the President on changes related to FEMA. The council will look at FEMA’s disaster response over the previous 4 years, compare it with state, local, and private sector responses, and examine public debate about FEMA reform. It will also gather input from people affected by natural disasters, researchers, governments, foundations, and nonprofit organizations.

14181.s: This order directs federal agencies to take steps to provide more water resources in Southern California and to help with disaster response in some areas. It tells agencies to speed up actions related to water delivery, wildfire response, housing help, debris removal, and road clearing. It also directs review of federal programs and funding tied to California land management, water supply, and disaster preparedness, and it limits certain federal preparedness grants for the City of Los Angeles from supporting illegal aliens.

14182.s: This order says the United States policy is to end the use of federal taxpayer dollars to fund or promote elective abortion, consistent with the Hyde Amendment. It directs the Office of Management and Budget to issue guidance for executive departments and agencies on how to carry out that policy. It also revokes two executive orders from 2022.

14183.s: This order says the military must set high standards for readiness, cohesion, honesty, humility, uniformity, and integrity. It directs the Defense Secretary to update medical standards, end invented and identification-based pronoun use, and issue guidance on sleeping, changing, and bathing facilities. It also revokes Executive Order 14004 and tells Defense and Homeland Security to carry out that revocation for the Coast Guard.

14184.s: This order tells the Defense Secretary or Homeland Security Secretary to make reinstatement available to military members who were discharged only for refusing the COVID-19 vaccine and who ask to return. It also allows reinstated members to go back to their former rank and receive full back pay, benefits, bonus payments, or other compensation. Service members who say in a written sworn statement that they left the service or let their service lapse rather than get vaccinated may also be allowed to return without a change in status, rank, or pay.

14185.s: This order directs the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security, including the Coast Guard, to operate free from preferences based on race or sex. It requires them to abolish DEI offices and related programs, and to review actions taken in pursuit of DEI initiatives. It also bars the Defense Department and the Armed Forces from promoting certain concepts, including divisive concepts, race or sex stereotyping, and gender ideology, and requires reviews of military schools and other defense academic institutions.

14186.s: This order directs the United States to deploy and maintain a next-generation missile defense shield. It says the shield should defend citizens and critical infrastructure against foreign aerial attack and protect the country’s secure second-strike capability. It also tells the Secretary of Defense to submit a plan, review Defense Department authorities and organization, and work on missile defense cooperation with allies and partners.

14187.s: This order says the U.S. will not fund, sponsor, promote, assist, or support the transition of a child from one sex to another. It tells federal agencies to change policies that rely on WPATH guidance, review research on care for minors with gender dysphoria, and take steps to end these medical treatments for children. It also directs changes to federal grants, TRICARE, and federal employee and postal health benefits to exclude coverage for pediatric transgender surgeries or hormone treatments.

14188.s: This order reaffirms the policy to combat anti-Semitism and directs federal agencies to use legal tools to prosecute, remove, or otherwise hold people accountable for unlawful anti-Semitic harassment and violence. It requires agency heads, including the Attorney General and the Secretary of Education, to report on laws, complaints, court cases, and other actions related to campus anti-Semitism. It also asks the Secretaries of State, Education, and Homeland Security to recommend ways for colleges to watch for and report activities by alien students and staff that may affect admissibility rules and lead to investigations or removal if warranted.

14189.s: This order creates a White House task force to plan and carry out a celebration of the 250th anniversary of American Independence. It says federal agencies should help with planning and report their work to the task force. It also reinstates earlier orders on the National Garden of American Heroes and on protecting American monuments from vandalism.

14190.s: This order directs federal agencies to prepare a plan to stop federal funding from supporting what it calls gender ideology and discriminatory equity ideology in K-12 schools. It also says agencies should protect parental rights under FERPA and the PPRA, and the Attorney General should work with state and local prosecutors on lawbreaking by K-12 teachers and school officials. The order reestablishes the 1776 Commission to promote patriotic education and support related programs and events. It also tells agencies to monitor compliance with a law requiring schools that get federal funds to hold a Constitution program for students.

14191.s: This order directs the Education Secretary to issue guidance on how states can use federal formula funds to support K-12 educational choice. It also tells the Education, Labor, Health and Human Services, Defense, and Interior secretaries to review grant or funding programs and report ways families could use them for schools or other educational options of their choice. The order focuses on parents, low-income working families, military-connected families, and families of students eligible for Bureau of Indian Education schools.

14192.s: This order directs federal agencies to cut regulations and identify at least 10 existing regulations for repeal when they propose a new one. It sets a policy that new regulations should be offset by lower costs from repealed rules, and it gives the Office of Management and Budget a role in setting cost limits and guidance. The order also defines “regulation” broadly but excludes military, national security, homeland security, foreign affairs, and immigration-related functions, plus some agency management rules.

14193.s: This order adds duties on many products of Canada to address illicit drugs and illegal migration across the northern border. Most Canadian products get a 25 percent duty, and energy or energy resources get a 10 percent duty, with some exceptions for goods already in transit. The duties apply to goods entered for consumption on or after February 4, 2025, and can be removed if Canada takes enough cooperative enforcement action.

14194.s: This order puts an additional 25 percent duty on articles that are products of Mexico, with some exceptions for goods already in transit. It says the tariffs apply to imports from Mexico and may be removed if the President determines that Mexico has taken enough steps to help address illegal migration and illicit drug trafficking. It also says the Secretary of Homeland Security can take actions needed to carry out the order.

14195.s: This order puts an extra 10 percent duty on articles that are products of the People’s Republic of China. It says the duties are tied to the flow of synthetic opioids and precursor chemicals linked to the opioid crisis. The order also says the duties can be removed if the President decides the PRC has taken enough action to help address the crisis.

14196.s: This order directs the Treasury Secretary and the Commerce Secretary to develop a plan for a United States sovereign wealth fund. The plan must cover funding methods, investment strategies, fund structure, and a governance model, and it must also review any legal issues, including whether legislation is needed. The order says the fund would be for the benefit of American citizens and would aim to lessen the burden of taxes on American families and small businesses.

14197.s: This order pauses the extra tariffs on products of Canada, including the higher rate for energy products, until March 4, 2025. It says the pause is to let officials assess whether the situation at the northern border has improved. During the pause, the Secretary of Homeland Security and other officials must continue reviewing the situation, and the President may restart the tariffs if the illegal migration and illicit drug crises worsen and Canada does not take enough steps.

14198.s: This order pauses the additional 25 percent tariff rate on products of Mexico until March 4, 2025, at 12:01 a.m. eastern time. During the pause, the Secretary of Homeland Security and other officials must keep assessing the situation at the southern border. If illegal migration and illicit drug crises worsen and Mexico does not take enough steps, the President may put the tariffs into effect.

14199.s: This order says the United States will not participate in the UN Human Rights Council and will not seek election to it. It also orders a review of U.S. membership in UNESCO and a broader review of international organizations, conventions, and treaties the United States supports. The order says executive departments and agencies may not use funds for UNRWA, and the United States will not fund UNRWA or the UN Human Rights Council.

14200.s: This order changes an earlier order about duties on covered articles from the People's Republic of China tied to the synthetic opioid supply chain. It says duty-free de minimis treatment can still apply to eligible covered articles for now, but it will stop once the Secretary of Commerce tells the President that systems are ready to fully and quickly collect the tariff revenue. It applies to covered articles that would otherwise qualify for de minimis treatment.

14201.s: This order directs federal agencies to enforce a policy that women's sports are reserved for women and that all-female athletic opportunities and locker rooms be protected. It tells the Education Department to review and, where appropriate, rescind federal funding for educational programs that do not follow this policy. It also directs the State and Homeland Security Departments to review policies on males seeking to enter the United States to participate in women's sports, and to work on international sports rules based on sex, not gender identity or testosterone reduction.

14202.s: This order sets up a task force in the Department of Justice to review actions by executive departments and agencies for unlawful anti-Christian policies, practices, or conduct. It directs the task force to recommend steps to revoke or end those policies and to suggest other actions to protect religious liberty. The task force must report to the President, and federal agencies must provide information when requested if allowed by law.

14203.s: This order says the United States will impose sanctions on certain International Criminal Court officials, employees, agents, and others who help ICC actions against protected persons. It blocks property and interests in property for covered people, limits donations and transactions with them, and suspends their entry into the United States, along with entry for some immediate family members. It also directs the Secretary of the Treasury and the Secretary of State to help carry it out and to report on additional people who should be covered.

14204.s: This order says the United States will not provide aid or assistance to South Africa while it continues the practices described in the order. It also directs agencies to work to resettle Afrikaner refugees escaping government-sponsored race-based discrimination, including racially discriminatory property confiscation. The Secretary of State and the Secretary of Homeland Security must take steps to prioritize humanitarian relief and refugee admission for Afrikaners in South Africa who are victims of unjust racial discrimination.

14205.s: This order creates the White House Faith Office within the Executive Office of the President. The office is meant to help faith-based entities, community organizations, and houses of worship serve families and communities, and to work on religious liberty matters. It also directs agencies to support the office, appoint faith liaisons where needed, and provide training and information on grants, religious liberty exceptions, and related issues.

14206.s: This order directs the Attorney General to review executive actions, rules, guidance, plans, international agreements, and other agency actions for possible infringements on Second Amendment rights. It also directs a review of firearms rules, agency classifications of firearms and ammunition, and the processing of applications to make, manufacture, transfer, or export firearms. The Attorney General must then prepare a proposed plan of action and work to finalize a process for implementation.

14207.s: This order directs the Office of Personnel Management to take the steps needed to eliminate the Federal Executive Institute. It also revokes earlier presidential and executive branch documents that established or required the institute. The order says it should be carried out under applicable law and based on available appropriations.

14208.s: This order makes it U.S. policy to end the use of paper straws. It directs federal agencies to stop buying paper straws and to stop providing them in agency buildings. It also directs a national strategy that would address policies against plastic straws and contracts with entities, including states, that ban or penalize plastic straw purchase or use.

14209.s: This order tells the Attorney General to review the rules and policies for investigations and enforcement under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act for 180 days. During that time, new FCPA investigations or enforcement actions should stop unless an exception is made. The Attorney General must review existing cases, issue updated guidance, and may extend the review for another 180 days.

14210.s: This order directs federal agencies to cut the size of the federal workforce through efficiency improvements and attrition. It sets a hiring ratio of no more than one new employee for every four employees who leave, with exceptions for public safety, immigration enforcement, and law enforcement. Agency heads must also plan for large-scale reductions in force, review positions that may be eliminated or consolidated, and consult with DOGE team leads on new hiring.

14211.s: This order says officers and employees who carry out U.S. foreign policy must do so under the President’s direction and authority. It says failure to faithfully implement the President’s policy can lead to professional discipline, including separation. It also directs the Secretary of State to reform the Foreign Service, including recruiting, performance, evaluation, retention, and training, and to revise or replace related manuals and guidance.

14212.s: This order creates the President’s Make America Healthy Again Commission, led by the Secretary of Health and Human Services. The commission must study childhood chronic disease and possible contributing causes, including diet, medical treatments, lifestyle, environmental factors, food production, and government policies. It must also give the President an assessment within 100 days and a strategy within 180 days. Federal health agencies must focus on reversing chronic disease and on research, treatment options, and policies tied to health and healthcare.

14213.s: This order creates the National Energy Dominance Council within the Executive Office of the President. The Council is told to advise the President on increasing energy production, improving permitting and regulation, and developing a National Energy Dominance Strategy. It also must review ways to expand energy production, including electricity capacity, energy infrastructure approvals, natural gas pipelines, reopened power plants, and Small Modular Nuclear Reactors. Agencies must cooperate with the Council and provide information and advice on policies that affect energy dominance.

14214.s: This order directs the Secretary of Education to issue guidance to schools and colleges about parental authority, religious freedom, disability accommodations, and equal protection as they relate to COVID-19 school mandates. It also requires a plan to end coercive COVID-19 school mandates and to list grants, contracts, and processes for stopping or taking back federal funds from schools that do not follow the guidance. The policy says discretionary federal funds should not support schools or institutions of higher education that require students to have a COVID-19 vaccination to attend in-person education.

14215.s: This order says all executive departments and agencies, including independent regulatory agencies, must send proposed and final significant regulatory actions to OIRA before they are published in the Federal Register. It directs OMB to set performance standards for independent agency heads, review their spending plans, and consult with them on policies and priorities. It also requires those agencies to create a White House Liaison position and says the President and Attorney General’s legal views control executive branch employees in their official duties.

14216.s: This order says the Administration’s policy is to help ensure reliable access to in vitro fertilization (IVF) and make treatment more affordable. It directs the Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy to submit recommendations within 90 days on protecting IVF access and reducing out-of-pocket and health plan costs. It affects Americans who need IVF, including men and women with fertility challenges.

14217.s: This order directs the federal government to reduce the size of the federal bureaucracy and eliminate non-statutory parts of certain government entities as allowed by law. It also tells agencies to limit staffing and functions at those entities to what law requires. The order revokes a 1961 presidential memorandum, directs steps to end the Federal Executive Boards, and moves to terminate the Presidential Management Fellows Program and several federal advisory committees.

14218.s: This order directs federal agencies to identify programs that let illegal aliens get cash or non-cash public benefits and to take steps, consistent with law, to align those programs with federal law. It also tells agencies to make sure federal payments to states and localities do not help subsidize or promote illegal immigration or support sanctuary policies. The order calls for stronger eligibility checks and for agencies to refer improper use of federal benefits to the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security.

14219.s: This order directs federal agencies to review regulations and identify ones that are unconstitutional, not backed by the best reading of a statute, or that impose costs, burdens, or other problems listed in the order. It tells agencies to seek to rescind or modify those regulations and to generally de-prioritize enforcement of rules that go beyond legal authority. It also says agencies should consult with DOGE Team Leads and OIRA on new regulations. The order does not apply to military, national security, homeland security, foreign affairs, or immigration-related functions, or to employee management matters.

14220.s: This order directs the Secretary of Commerce to investigate how imports of copper, scrap copper, and copper derivative products affect national security. The review covers raw copper, copper concentrates, refined copper, copper alloys, scrap copper, and derivative products. It also looks at whether tariffs, quotas, export controls, or incentives to increase domestic production may be needed, and it affects federal agencies involved in defense, energy, the interior, and commerce.

14221.s: This order directs federal agencies to speed up and enforce healthcare price transparency rules. It requires them to work on getting actual prices, not estimates, and to make pricing information standardized and easier to compare across hospitals and health plans. It affects patients, hospitals, and health plans.

14222.s: This order tells federal agencies to track payments for covered contracts and grants and record a brief written reason for each payment. It also requires agencies to review existing covered contracts and grants, review contracting policies and personnel, and limit new contracting approvals during that review. Agencies must also justify federally funded travel for conferences or other non-essential purposes, freeze most agency employee credit cards for 30 days, and review federal real property for possible disposition. The order does not apply to certain law enforcement, immigration enforcement, military, public safety, intelligence, and other exempted matters.

14223.s: This order directs the Secretary of Commerce to investigate whether imports of timber, lumber, and their derivative products threaten national security. The review must look at domestic demand, domestic production, foreign supply chains, subsidies, trade practices, and whether tariffs, quotas, or other measures are needed. It also requires consultation with the Secretary of Defense and a report to the President with findings and recommendations.

14224.s: This order designates English as the official language of the United States. It revokes Executive Order 13166, but says it does not require or direct any change in agency services. Agency heads are not required to stop documents, products, or other services in languages other than English. The Attorney General must rescind policy guidance issued under Executive Order 13166 and provide updated guidance.

14225.s: This order directs federal agencies to speed up timber production, forest management, and wildfire risk reduction projects. It tells the Interior and Agriculture Departments to issue new guidance, submit legislative proposals, set a timber sales target for the next 4 years, and complete several Endangered Species Act reviews. It also tells agencies to cut permitting delays and review rules and policies that place an undue burden on timber production.

14226.s: This order changes a prior order about duties on covered articles tied to the flow of illicit drugs across the northern border. It says duty-free de minimis treatment is available for otherwise eligible covered articles under sections (a) and (b). That treatment will end when the Secretary of Commerce tells the President that adequate systems are in place to fully and quickly process and collect the tariff revenue for those articles.

14227.s: This order changes a previous order about duties at the southern border. It keeps duty-free "de minimis" treatment available for otherwise eligible covered articles. That treatment will stop when the Secretary of Commerce tells the President that there are adequate systems to fully and quickly process and collect the tariff revenue for those covered articles.

14228.s: This order raises the ad valorem tariff on products of the People's Republic of China from 10 percent to 20 percent. It says the change is being made because the government of China has not taken adequate steps to help stop the flow of synthetic opioids, including fentanyl, to the United States. The order affects articles that are products of China.

14229.s: This order renames the Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge as the Jocelyn Nungaray National Wildlife Refuge. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to update procedures, make the renaming official, and make sure Federal maps, contracts, and other documents use the new name. The order says the renaming is to honor Jocelyn Nungaray and permanently commemorate her life.

14230.s: This order directs agencies to suspend any active security clearances held by people at Perkins Coie while those clearances are reviewed. It also tells agencies to stop providing certain government goods, property, materials, and services to the firm where allowed by law, and to review contracts with Perkins Coie or with entities that do business with it. The order also calls for reviews and investigations of large law firms for race-based and sex-based non-discrimination compliance, and it limits access to federal buildings and federal hiring of Perkins Coie employees in some cases.

14231.s: This order changes some tariffs on goods from Canada under earlier trade rules. It removes the extra duty from certain Canadian goods that enter free of duty under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade rules, and it lowers the extra duty on potash to 10 percent instead of 25 percent. The changes apply to goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption on or after March 7, 2025.

14232.s: This order changes some tariffs on goods from Mexico. It says certain goods that enter free of duty under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement will not face the extra duty, and the extra duty on some potash will drop to 10 percent instead of 25 percent. The changes apply to goods entered for consumption on or after March 7, 2025.

14233.s: This order directs the Treasury Department to create a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a United States Digital Asset Stockpile. The Bitcoin reserve would hold certain bitcoin the government has forfeited and would not be sold. The digital asset stockpile would hold other forfeited digital assets, and agencies must report any government digital assets they hold and review whether they can be transferred to these accounts.

14234.s: This order creates the White House Task Force on the FIFA World Cup 2026. The Task Force will help plan, organize, and carry out events around the 2025 FIFA Club World Cup and the 2026 FIFA World Cup. It includes several cabinet officials and other White House and agency leaders, and the Department of Homeland Security will house it and provide support if funds are available.

14235.s: This order directs the Secretary of Education to propose changes to the Public Service Loan Forgiveness rules. The changes would make some organizations ineligible if they have a substantial illegal purpose. It lists activities such as helping break federal immigration laws, supporting terrorism, child abuse, illegal discrimination, and certain state law violations.

14236.s: This order revokes a list of earlier executive actions, memoranda, and presidential determinations from the prior administration. The revoked actions covered public health, foreign policy, LGBTQ+ rights, the minimum wage for federal contractors, energy supply, infant formula, clean energy, biotechnology, defense supply chains, worker rights, tribal funding, apprenticeships, and investment in American workers. It says the revocations are meant to restore common sense to the Federal Government and unleash the potential of American citizens.

14237.s: This order directs agencies to review and suspend active security clearances held by people at Paul Weiss and Mark Pomerantz, pending a review of whether they are in the national interest. It also tells agencies to identify government goods and services provided to Paul Weiss and, where allowed by law, stop providing them. Federal contractors may be required to disclose any business they do with Paul Weiss, and agencies are told to review contracts with Paul Weiss or with entities that do business with it. The order also limits official access to federal buildings for Paul Weiss employees in some cases and tells agencies to refrain from hiring them unless there is a waiver.

14238.s: This order continues reducing parts of the federal bureaucracy the President has determined are unnecessary. It directs the non-statutory components and functions of several federal entities to be eliminated to the maximum extent allowed by law, and says those entities should keep only the minimum statutory functions and staff required by law. It also requires their heads to report compliance and directs budget reviewers to reject funding requests that do not fit the order.

14239.s: This executive order tells the federal government to put more responsibility for preparedness on State and local governments and individuals. It orders a new National Resilience Strategy and reviews of critical infrastructure, continuity, and preparedness policies. It also calls for a National Risk Register to identify and quantify risks to national infrastructure and for changes to how the federal government explains its preparedness roles.

14240.s: This order directs federal agencies to propose moving domestic procurement for common goods and services to the General Services Administration, where allowed by law. It also directs the Administrator of General Services to submit a plan for the government to buy common goods and services across domestic components of the government. The order gives the Administrator the role of executive agent for government-wide information technology acquisition contracts and calls for reducing duplication and inefficiencies in those contracts.

14241.s:
This order directs federal agencies to speed up permits and approvals for mineral production projects in the United States. It also calls for recommendations on the Mining Act of 1872 and for federal land plans to give priority to mineral production and related uses.

The order tells agencies to identify federal lands and sites that may be suitable for mineral production and for leasing to private entities. It also directs steps to support private and public investment, including use of defense and development finance tools, loans, and other assistance for domestic mineral production.

14242.s: This order directs the Secretary of Education to take steps to close the Department of Education and return authority over education to the states and local communities. It says services, programs, and benefits should continue without interruption during that process. It also says federal education funds must follow federal law and administration policy, including ending illegal discrimination labeled as "diversity, equity, and inclusion" or similar terms and programs promoting gender ideology.

14243.s: This order directs agency heads to give certain federal officials full and prompt access to unclassified agency records, data, software systems, and information technology systems to help identify and eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse. It also requires agencies to rescind or change rules that block sharing of unclassified information and to review data access and classification policies. The order says the federal government should have access to data from state programs that receive federal funding, and it gives the Secretary of Labor and designees access to unemployment data and related payment records.

14244.s: This order revokes Executive Order 14237 from March 14, 2025, which had addressed Paul Weiss. It says Paul Weiss acknowledged wrongdoing by a former partner and agreed to policy changes on client selection, attorney hiring, pro bono matters, and merit-based hiring, promotion, and retention. It also says the firm will dedicate the equivalent of $40 million in pro bono legal services during the President’s term to support certain causes.

14245.s: This order says a 25 percent tariff may be imposed on goods imported into the United States from any country that imports Venezuelan oil, either directly or through third parties. The Secretary of State, with other officials, decides whether the tariff will apply to a country and can also decide when it ends. If the tariff is imposed on China, it also applies to Hong Kong and Macau.

14246.s: This order targets Jenner & Block and directs agencies to review security clearances held by its employees and to limit some government access and contacts with them. It also tells agencies to review contracts involving Jenner or entities that do business with Jenner, and to take steps to end certain contracts where allowed by law. The order says agencies should, where permitted, stop hiring Jenner employees unless there is a waiver.

14247.s: This order directs federal departments and agencies to move Federal payments and receipts from paper checks to electronic payments, to the extent allowed by law. It covers federal disbursements and payments to the Federal Government, including benefits, vendor payments, tax refunds, fees, fines, loans, and taxes. It also creates exceptions for some people and situations, including those without access to banking services or electronic payment systems, certain emergency payments, and some national security or law enforcement activities.

14248.s: The order directs federal agencies to require documentary proof of United States citizenship on the national mail voter registration form and to help states verify the citizenship or immigration status of people registering to vote or already registered. It also tells agencies to share certain federal records with state and local election officials, review voter registration lists, and provide information on foreign nationals who indicated they registered or voted in an election. The order requires new voting system standards that avoid barcodes or quick-response codes in the vote-counting process except when needed for people with disabilities and calls for a voter-verifiable paper record. It also directs the Attorney General to step up enforcement of election laws and coordinate with states on suspected election crimes.

14249.s: This order directs the Treasury Department and OMB to strengthen checks on federal payments to help prevent fraud and improper payments. It requires agencies to share more payment information, follow Treasury verification steps, and update some privacy records to allow certain disclosures for fraud detection and recovery. It also directs agencies to consolidate core financial systems and move disbursing functions to Treasury when possible, which would affect federal agencies that handle payments and financial records.

14250.s: This order directs agencies to review and suspend active security clearances held by people at WilmerHale, if allowed by law. It also tells agencies to identify and, where permitted, stop providing WilmerHale with government goods, property, material, services, and certain access to federal buildings and employees. Government contractors must disclose any business they do with WilmerHale, and agencies must review contracts with WilmerHale or with entities that do business with it. Agencies are also directed to limit hiring of WilmerHale employees, unless there is a waiver.

14251.s: This order excludes many listed federal agencies and agency subdivisions from federal labor-management relations coverage because they are found to do intelligence, counterintelligence, investigative, or national security work. It also gives the Secretaries of Defense and Veterans Affairs authority to suspend the rules for certain subdivisions if they certify it can be done consistently with national security requirements. The Secretary of Transportation is given authority to exclude subdivisions of the Department of Transportation, including the Federal Aviation Administration, and to suspend certain rules for Transportation facilities outside the 50 States and the District of Columbia.

14252.s: This order sets up a task force to work with local officials on safety in Washington, D.C. It calls for more federal help with immigration enforcement, crime reduction, transit fare evasion, and enforcement of public-safety and quality-of-life laws. It also directs the Secretary of the Interior to develop a program to beautify the District and orders cleanup of graffiti and homeless or vagrant encampments on certain federal land.

14253.s:
This order directs the Vice President and other officials to work on the Smithsonian Institution, its museums, education and research centers, and the National Zoo. It tells them to seek to remove what the order calls improper ideology and to work with Congress on future Smithsonian funding rules.

It also directs the Secretary of the Interior to improve infrastructure at Independence National Historical Park and to review monuments, memorials, statues, and markers under the Department of the Interior. The review is meant to restore pre-existing displays when appropriate and to make sure these properties do not contain content that disparages Americans or presents what the order calls a false reconstruction of American history.

14254.s: This order directs federal agencies to act against unfair practices in the live concert and entertainment market. It tells the Attorney General and the FTC to enforce competition laws, enforce the Better Online Tickets Sales Act, and look at price transparency and unfair conduct in the secondary ticketing market. It also tells the Treasury Secretary and Attorney General to make sure ticket scalpers follow the Internal Revenue Code and other applicable law.

14255.s: This order creates a United States Investment Accelerator inside the Department of Commerce. It is meant to help investors with federal regulatory processes, reduce regulatory burdens where allowed by law, and work with state governments to reduce barriers to domestic and foreign investment. It also gives the office responsibility for the CHIPS Program Office and tells it to look for ways in federal law to assist foreign and domestic investors while protecting national security.

14256.s: This order ends duty-free de minimis treatment for certain low-value goods from the People’s Republic of China and Hong Kong, including international postal packages, sent to the United States on or after May 2, 2025. It requires those shipments to pay duties under one of two methods: 30 percent of the item’s value, or a fixed duty per postal item. It also requires carriers to collect and remit the duties, keep a bond, and report shipment information to Customs and Border Protection.

14258.s: This order extends the delay on enforcing the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act until June 19, 2025. During that time, the Department of Justice may not enforce the law or impose penalties against any entity for noncompliance, including for distributing, maintaining, or updating a covered app. The Attorney General must issue guidance and letters saying there was no violation and no liability for covered conduct during the stated period and before this order.

14259.s: This order raises duties on certain goods from the People’s Republic of China after China said it would impose tariffs on goods from the United States. It changes the tariff rate from 34% to 84% for covered goods entered on or after April 9, 2025. It also raises duties on low-value imports, including the ad valorem rate and the per postal item duty. These changes affect imports from China and people or businesses bringing in those goods.

14260.s: This order directs the Attorney General to identify state and local laws, regulations, policies, and practices that burden the identification, development, siting, production, or use of domestic energy resources and may be unconstitutional, preempted by federal law, or otherwise unenforceable. It tells the Attorney General to prioritize laws dealing with "climate change," "environmental, social, and governance" initiatives, "environmental justice," carbon or "greenhouse gas" emissions, and carbon penalties or taxes. It also directs action to stop enforcement of state laws and civil actions that are found to be illegal.

14261.s: This order directs federal agencies to support coal production, coal leasing on federal lands, coal exports, and coal-fired electricity generation. It also tells agencies to review and possibly revise or rescind policies that discourage coal. The order asks agencies to look at coal resources, coal use for steel and artificial intelligence data centers, and ways to speed up coal technology.

14262.s: This order directs the Energy Secretary to speed up the process for issuing emergency orders when a temporary power supply interruption is needed to avoid a complete grid failure. It also requires a method for studying reserve margins in regions of the bulk power system and publishing that analysis on the Energy Department website. The order says the government should use available power generation resources and identify generation resources that are critical to system reliability.

14263.s: This order targets Susman Godfrey and directs agencies to review and suspend any active security clearances held by its employees, pending review. It also tells agencies to identify and, where allowed by law, stop providing government goods, property, material, and services to the firm. Federal contractors may have to disclose business they do with Susman Godfrey, and agencies are to review contracts with the firm and may try to end them where allowed. Agencies are also told to limit official access and engagement with Susman Godfrey employees and generally refrain from hiring them unless there is a waiver.

14264.s: This order directs the Secretary of Energy to publish a notice rescinding the 2021 regulation that defines "showerhead." It also rescinds the definition of "showerhead" in the federal code. The rescission takes effect 30 days after the notice is published.

14265.s: This order directs the Defense Department to speed up defense buying and update how it acquires weapons, equipment, and services. It requires plans to use faster buying methods, cut extra reviews, and change rules and training for the acquisition workforce. It also orders a review of major defense programs to find ones that are behind schedule, over cost, unable to meet key performance needs, or not aligned with the Secretary of Defense's priorities.

14266.s: This order changes tariff rates on imported goods in response to other countries’ actions. It keeps the higher rate on goods from China and raises it to 125 percent, while goods from other listed trading partners are subject to a 10 percent additional tariff for 90 days. It also increases certain tariffs and postal item duties on low-value imports from China.

14267.s: This order starts a review of federal regulations that may create monopolies, add barriers for new market entrants, limit competition, or create unnecessary licensing or procurement burdens. Agency heads must give lists of such regulations and recommend rescinding or changing them, and the public may comment on the identified rules. The Office of Management and Budget will then consider whether to add proposed changes to the Unified Regulatory Agenda.

14268.s: This order directs changes to the foreign defense sales system to improve accountability, transparency, and speed. It tells the Secretaries of State and Defense to review restrictions and update lists for defense items and priority partners, and to work with Congress on notification processes. It also calls for a plan to improve tracking of export license requests and foreign military sales, and to create a single electronic tracking system.

14269.s: This order directs federal officials to prepare a Maritime Action Plan to rebuild U.S. maritime industries and workforce. It calls for reports and proposals on shipbuilding, cargo fees and tariffs, a Maritime Security Trust Fund, financial incentives, and maritime prosperity zones. It also directs agencies to look at training more mariners and reviewing federal programs that support shipping and shipbuilding.

14270.s: This order tells certain agencies to add a sunset date to covered energy regulations, so those rules must be reviewed and may expire unless they are extended. It applies to the Environmental Protection Agency, the Department of Energy, FERC, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and certain Interior and Army offices. It also says new covered regulations should include a sunset date, unless exempted, and it does not apply to regulatory permitting regimes authorized by statute.

14271.s: This order directs federal agencies to buy commercially available products and services to the maximum extent practicable. It also requires agencies to review open requests for non-commercial products or services and justify why those items are needed. Approval officials must review these requests, may seek input from the Office of Management and Budget, and must report on compliance and progress.

14272.s: This order directs the Secretary of Commerce to investigate whether imports of processed critical minerals and derivative products threaten national security. It defines those minerals and products and asks for a report with recommendations on possible tariffs, import restrictions, safeguards, and ways to encourage domestic production, processing, and recycling. The order affects imports of these materials and the industries that use them.

14273.s: This executive order directs federal officials to take steps aimed at lowering prescription drug prices for American patients and taxpayers. It calls for changes to Medicare drug pricing, Medicare Part D premiums, Medicaid drug rebates, and payment for high-cost drugs and biological products. It also directs work on making insulin and injectable epinephrine available at lower prices for some low-income people, improving drug importation, speeding approval of generics and biosimilars, and increasing transparency for pharmacy benefit manager fees.

14274.s: This order revokes two older executive orders on Federal office space management. It directs the Administrator of General Services to start changing the related regulations and take other steps needed to match this order. Agencies that use federally owned or leased space under other legal authority must follow this order as far as the law allows.

14275.s: This order directs changes to the Federal Acquisition Regulation, which sets rules for federal procurement. It tells agencies to work with the Office of Federal Public Procurement Policy and the FAR Council to remove rules that are not required by statute or needed for sound procurement, and to make the system simpler and easier to use. It also calls for agency supplemental rules to be aligned with this reform and for some non-statutory provisions to be considered for sunset unless renewed.

14276.s: This order directs federal officials to review seafood regulations and reduce burdens on commercial fishing, aquaculture, and fish processing industries. It also calls for steps to update fisheries data, expand exempted fishing permits, and use more reliable technology in fishery assessments. The order tells officials to develop seafood trade and import strategies, review foreign seafood trade practices, and look at marine national monuments that could be opened to commercial fishing.

14277.s: This order sets a policy to promote AI literacy and proficiency by adding AI into education, training educators, and giving youth early exposure to AI concepts and technology. It creates a White House task force to carry out the order and coordinate federal efforts on AI education. It also directs plans for a presidential AI challenge, K-12 AI resources, teacher training, and support for AI-related apprenticeships and student courses.

14278.s: This order directs the Labor, Commerce, and Education Secretaries to review federal workforce programs and recommend ways to consolidate, reform, redirect, or eliminate them. It also calls for a plan to reach and surpass 1 million new active apprentices and to expand Registered Apprenticeships into new industries and occupations. The order requires more transparency on workforce program results, including earnings and employment data, for programs and credentials supported by federal funds.

14279.s: This order directs the Education Department to change how higher education accreditors are recognized and reviewed. It says accreditors should be held accountable if they require unlawful discrimination, and it directs investigations of law school and medical school accreditors. It also calls for accreditation rules that focus on high-quality academic programs, student outcomes, intellectual diversity, and less burdensome accreditation processes.

14280.s: This order directs the Department of Education to issue new guidance on school discipline and racial discrimination under Title VI. It also tells the department to take action against local and state education agencies that do not comply, and to work with governors and state attorneys general on preventing racial discrimination in school discipline. The Secretary of Defense must also issue a revised school discipline code for children of military-service families.

14281.s: This order directs federal agencies to eliminate the use of disparate-impact liability as much as possible. It revokes certain past approvals of Department of Justice Title VI regulations and tells agencies to deprioritize enforcement of laws and rules that include disparate-impact liability. It also directs reviews of pending investigations, civil suits, consent judgments, and permanent injunctions that rely on that theory, and asks for guidance to employers about equal access to employment.

14282.s: This order directs the Secretary of Education to enforce foreign funding disclosure rules for higher education institutions. It requires more complete and timely reporting of foreign funds, including the true source and purpose of the money, and calls for audits and investigations when needed. It also says federal grant funds should not be provided to schools that do not comply with these disclosure requirements.

14283.s: This order creates a White House Initiative on Historically Black Colleges and Universities to work with federal agencies and outside partners. It directs the initiative to help HBCUs improve education, infrastructure, research, student success, and access to federal funding. It also creates a President’s Board of Advisors on HBCUs and requires an annual progress report to the President. The order revokes a prior executive order on HBCUs and tells the EPA to end a related advisory council.

14284.s: This order changes how federal agencies review employees in probationary and trial periods. Agencies must decide whether keeping these employees would serve the public interest before their appointments are finalized, and they must certify that in writing. If the agency does not make that certification, the employee’s service ends at the end of the probationary or trial period. It also applies new review steps and rules to agencies and affected federal employees.

14285.s: This order directs federal agencies to speed up review of permits and licenses for seabed mineral exploration and commercial recovery, and to set up expedited permit processes for seabed mineral resources in the United States Outer Continental Shelf. It also calls for reports and plans on mapping seabed areas, identifying critical minerals from seabed resources, and reviewing ways to support domestic processing. The order tells agencies to work with allies and partners on seabed mineral exploration, extraction, processing, and environmental monitoring, and to look at tools for financing and supply chain support.

14286.s: This order tells the Transportation Department to enforce English-language rules for commercial motor vehicle drivers. It directs the department to rescind old guidance, issue new inspection guidance, and revise out-of-service rules so a violation of the English requirement can remove a driver from service. It also orders reviews of non-domiciled commercial driver's licenses and steps to verify domestic and international commercial driving credentials.

14287.s: This order directs federal officials to publish and update a list of state and local “sanctuary jurisdictions” that obstruct federal immigration law enforcement. It says federal agencies should identify federal funds to those jurisdictions for possible suspension or termination, and it directs the Attorney General and Homeland Security Secretary to pursue legal remedies against jurisdictions that stay in defiance of federal law. It also calls for guidance to check eligibility for federal public benefits in sanctuary jurisdictions and for action against state and local laws that favor aliens over American citizens.

14288.s: This order directs federal agencies to support State and local law enforcement in policing crime and protecting citizens. It calls for legal defense and indemnification for officers who incur expenses or liabilities while doing their jobs, more training, pay, benefits, legal protections, and better crime data. It also directs the review of certain federal consent decrees and asks for more use of military and national security assets to assist law enforcement. It targets State and local officials whose actions unlawfully block law enforcement or involve discrimination or civil-rights violations that restrict police activity or endanger citizens.

14289.s: This order changes how certain tariffs on imported articles are applied so the same article does not face stacked tariffs from the listed tariff actions. It applies to tariffs on imported automobiles and parts, imports from the northern and southern border orders, and tariffs on aluminum and steel. The order also applies retroactively to covered entries made on or after March 4, 2025, and any refunds will follow customs procedures and applicable law.

14290.s: This order directs the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and federal agencies to stop direct and indirect federal funding for NPR and PBS. It tells the CPB Board to cancel existing direct funding to the maximum extent allowed by law and to change its grant rules to bar funding for NPR and PBS. It also directs agencies to look for any remaining grants or contracts with NPR or PBS and check whether they are complying with their agreements. The Secretary of Health and Human Services must also review whether NPR and PBS are complying with the rule against employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, or sex.

14291.s: This order creates the Religious Liberty Commission. The Commission will have up to 14 members appointed by the President, along with three ex officio members, and it will be advised by three smaller boards of religious leaders, lay leaders, and legal experts. It will study religious liberty in America, current threats to it, and ways to protect it, and it will advise the White House Faith Office and the Domestic Policy Council. The Commission is set to end on July 4, 2026, unless the President extends it.

14292.s: This order directs federal agencies to stop funding certain dangerous gain-of-function research and to suspend some federally funded research until new policy is finished. It also requires updated rules for oversight, nucleic acid screening, and public reporting of covered research. The order tells officials to develop a strategy to govern, limit, and track similar research that is not federally funded. It also adds contract and grant terms that can lead to loss of federal funding if the rules are broken.

14293.s: This order directs federal agencies to streamline rules and reviews for domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing. It tells Health and Human Services, the FDA, the EPA, and the Army Corps of Engineers to review and update regulations, reduce duplicative or unnecessary requirements, and speed permitting and approval. It also calls for more routine inspections of overseas manufacturing facilities involved in the supply of U.S. medicines and public reporting on those inspections.

14294.s: This order tells federal agencies to review criminal regulatory offenses and report them to the Office of Management and Budget. It says agencies should give clear notice when a rule can lead to criminal penalties, explain the law and mental state needed, and favor civil or administrative enforcement when appropriate. It also says enforcement of immigration laws and regulations, and laws or regulations related to national security or defense, are not covered by this order.

14295.s: This order directs the Archivist and the Government Publishing Office to reduce delays in publishing items in the Federal Register. It also requires reports on average publication times and a review of fee schedules so fees are based on actual publication costs and reflect increased efficiencies. It affects the Office of the Federal Register, the Government Publishing Office, and executive departments and agencies that pay to publish rules.

14296.s: This order directs the Department of Veterans Affairs to create a National Center for Warrior Independence at the West Los Angeles VA Campus. It says homeless veterans in the Los Angeles area and around the nation can seek care, benefits, and services there, and it tells the department to help them get housing, substance abuse or addiction treatment, and work and community support. It also directs the Department of Housing and Urban Development to use vouchers to support homeless veterans, and it orders steps to restore accountability and improve care and services for veterans.

14297.s: This order directs federal agencies to work toward most-favored-nation pricing for prescription drugs and biologics for American patients. It tells the Secretary of Health and Human Services to communicate price targets, help set up direct-to-consumer sales at that price, and take further steps if significant progress is not made. It also directs other agencies to review foreign pricing practices, consider importation, and look at enforcement actions and drug approvals if needed.

14298.s: This order changes tariff rates on goods from the People’s Republic of China, including Hong Kong and Macau. It sets an additional 10 percent ad valorem duty on those imports and suspends some higher duties for 90 days. It also lowers one duty on low-value imports from 120 percent to 54 percent and keeps the $100 duty on each postal item containing those goods.

14299.s: This order directs federal agencies to speed the development, deployment, and export of advanced nuclear reactor technologies for national security and energy needs. It requires the Department of Defense and Department of Energy to support nuclear reactors at military installations and DOE sites, including sites for AI data centers and other critical needs. It also directs the government to identify uranium and plutonium that can be used for fuel, provide HALEU for certain private projects, and promote more nuclear exports and cooperation with other countries.

14300.s: This order directs the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to reorganize its structure, staffing, regulations, and basic operations. It says the NRC should make license applications move faster, reduce some personnel and functions, and create a team to draft new regulations. It also directs the NRC to revise radiation limits, environmental rules, reactor security rules, and the licensing process for new reactor designs, microreactors, and modular reactors. The order affects the NRC and people or companies seeking licenses for nuclear reactors and related activities.

14301.s: This order directs the Department of Energy to speed up review, approval, and deployment of advanced reactors under its control. It tells the Secretary of Energy to define what counts as a qualified test reactor and to change Department rules so these reactors can be operational at Department-owned or controlled sites within 2 years after a complete application. It also creates a pilot program for reactor construction and operation outside the National Laboratories and requires at least three reactors to be approved under that program. The order says the Department should also streamline its environmental reviews under NEPA.

14302.s: This order directs federal agencies to speed up nuclear energy production, fuel supply, licensing, and workforce training. It calls for plans to expand uranium conversion and enrichment, change how surplus plutonium and spent nuclear fuel are handled, and support nuclear fuel supply chains. It also tells agencies to help restart, finish, uprate, or build nuclear plants and to expand training and apprenticeships for nuclear energy jobs.

14303.s: This order directs federal agencies to use and communicate scientific information in a transparent, rigorous, and unbiased way. It requires agencies and employees to avoid scientific misconduct, disclose data and models for certain influential scientific information, and clearly state uncertainties and assumptions when using science in decisions. It also tells agencies to update their scientific integrity policies, review some prior actions and policies, and set up internal processes to handle alleged violations.

14304.s: This order tells the Federal Aviation Administration to repeal the ban on overland supersonic flight and remove other rules that limit supersonic aviation. It also directs the FAA to create noise certification standards and propose new rules for supersonic aircraft noise. The order asks federal agencies to coordinate research on supersonic aircraft and to work with other countries and foreign aviation authorities on shared rules and safety agreements.

14305.s: This order directs federal agencies to strengthen control over U.S. airspace and protect the public, critical infrastructure, mass gatherings, military sites, and some government installations from drone threats. It creates a task force to review drone rules and recommend actions, and it directs the FAA to move forward with rulemaking on restricting drone flights over certain facilities. It also directs the Attorney General and other agencies to improve enforcement, detection, tracking, and identification of drones and drone signals, and to help state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies get related grants and information.

14306.s: This order changes earlier cybersecurity orders and directs agencies to take new steps on software security, patching, and post-quantum cryptography. It also tells agencies to share certain cyber defense research data, manage artificial intelligence software vulnerabilities, and update policy for federal networks. In addition, it directs steps for consumer Internet-of-Things products to carry United States Cyber Trust Mark labeling and changes sanctions rules to refer to foreign persons.

14307.s: This order directs agencies to speed up the safe use of drones in the national airspace and to support routine drone operations. It tells the Department of Transportation and the FAA to propose a rule for beyond visual line of sight drone flights, use AI tools to review waiver applications, and start an eVTOL pilot program. It also tells agencies to favor U.S.-made drones, secure the drone supply chain, and promote the export of American-made civil drones. The Department of Defense is directed to prioritize drones made by United States companies for military use and training.

14308.s: This order directs the Interior and Agriculture Departments to consolidate their wildland fire programs and improve how federal wildfire offices, budgets, and research are used. It also tells federal agencies to work with state, local, tribal, and community partners on wildfire preparedness, response, and land management. The order calls for a technology roadmap, more use of satellite data, and reviews of rules, prescribed fires, fire retardant, and other policies that may affect wildfire prevention and response.

14309.s: This order puts parts of the United States-United Kingdom trade deal into effect.
